# Kevin Warsh, the Fed, and Gold Prices in 2026

BY [MUFLIH HIDAYAT](https://discoveryalert.com.au/author/muflih-hidayat/) ON JULY 19, 2026

![Kevin Worsh Fed and gold prices outlook](https://discoveryalert.com.au/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/be2dacb7-9d88-47d7-9ea0-0c3ab2590ee7-1024x572.jpg)

## The Federal Reserve's Return as Gold's Dominant Force

Monetary policy cycles, not headlines, have historically produced the most durable moves in precious metals. While war, trade friction, and supply disruptions periodically seize control of gold pricing, the underlying gravitational field always traces back to one institution: the Federal Reserve. The relationship between Kevin Warsh Fed and gold prices has become the defining question for precious metals investors in 2026, and understanding this dynamic is not just academically useful — it is the difference between reacting to noise and positioning ahead of signal.

After a turbulent stretch in which geopolitical forces, tariff regimes, and extraordinary physical demand drove gold and silver markets with unusual independence from the Fed, that era has closed. Central bank policy has re-established itself as the dominant pricing variable, and a new figure at its helm is forcing investors to completely reassess their assumptions.

### When big ASX news breaks, our subscribers know first

## Gold Price Drivers Have Shifted: Understanding the New Hierarchy

### From Geopolitics Back to Monetary Policy

Not every driver of gold prices carries equal weight at every moment. Analysts broadly recognise three forces that compete for influence over precious metals pricing: monetary policy, geopolitical risk, and speculative momentum. Their relative dominance shifts across market cycles.

| Period | Primary Driver | Secondary Driver | Gold Trend |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2023 to Early 2024 | Fed rate expectations | Real yield compression | Bullish |
| Mid 2024 to 2025 | Geopolitical risk and tariff regimes | Physical demand and stockpiling | Volatile and Bullish |
| 2026 (present) | Fed Chair transition and monetary stance | Dollar strength | Bearish correction |

Between 2024 and 2025, supply chain disruptions, cross-border gold stockpiling, and questions around physical asset custody redirected trader attention away from Fed signals. Retail participation surged. Leverage compounded. Silver, in particular, reached price levels without modern precedent as industrial demand intersected with speculative positioning and logistical shortages.

That environment produced powerful but ultimately short-lived momentum. Momentum, by its nature, has a finite lifespan. As those distortions faded, monetary policy reclaimed the seat it never truly vacated. Furthermore, the [gold price forecast](https://discoveryalert.com.au/gold-price-forecast-2025-upward-momentum-geopolitical-economic/) heading into this period had already signalled upward momentum that was increasingly dependent on the Fed's directional lean.

### The Signal That Started the Bull Market

To understand where gold stands today, it is worth revisiting where the current bull cycle actually originated. Following a prolonged period of elevated interest rates designed to suppress post-pandemic inflation, markets began to shift their expectations well before any formal policy adjustment was announced.

The catalytic moment came when Fed Governor Chris Waller indicated in a press conference that rate reductions were being considered. Markets responded immediately. Gold caught that forward signal and entered a sustained uptrend that predated any actual policy change by months.

> **Core Insight:** Precious metals function as forward-pricing mechanisms. They respond to expectations, not events. The most profitable positioning in that cycle came from identifying the Fed's directional lean and aligning with it before rate decisions were formalised.

That lesson is directly relevant today. The question is no longer what the Fed has done, but what Kevin Warsh is likely to do — and whether markets have correctly priced his actual philosophy.

## Who Is Kevin Warsh and Why Does His Appointment Reshape the Gold Outlook?

### A Philosophical Departure from the Powell Era

When President Trump nominated Kevin Warsh to replace Jerome Powell as Federal Reserve Chair in early 2026, prevailing market consensus coalesced around a specific expectation: that Warsh would function as a politically aligned, rate-accommodative steward of the economy. The logic was straightforward. Trump had been openly critical of Powell's approach, and the assumption was that his chosen successor would be more willing to keep financial conditions loose.

That consensus proved costly for those who held it. According to [reporting from Forbes](https://www.forbes.com/sites/brandonkochkodin/2026/01/30/trumps-fed-pick-warsh-sets-off-the-worst-day-for-gold-and-silver-since-the-1980s/), Warsh's nomination triggered the worst single day for gold and silver since the 1980s — a stark illustration of how dramatically the market had mispriced his appointment.

Warsh's opening posture on inflation was aggressive, his language on institutional reform was pointed, and his overall stance diverged sharply from the accommodative trajectory the market had priced in. Rate cut expectations that were embedded in gold pricing before the appointment quickly reversed. Within weeks, market participants had shifted from anticipating one to two rate cuts in 2026 to pricing in the possibility of one to two rate hikes before year-end.

> **Key Insight:** Markets priced in a dovish loyalist. What arrived was an institutionally aggressive inflation hawk. That mispricing created one of the sharpest gold corrections in recent memory.

### Warsh's Intellectual Framework on Monetary Policy

Warsh's views on how central banks should operate are not new. He has long argued that the Fed's practice of telegraphing its rate intentions through forward guidance created a form of market dependency that reduced policy flexibility, distorted asset pricing, and ultimately undermined the credibility of monetary institutions.

His position is that price stability is not a flexible target to be balanced against other considerations — it is a foundational institutional commitment. This contrasts with the Powell-era framework of data-dependent gradualism, in which the Fed consistently signalled its intentions far in advance and adjusted course incrementally based on incoming data.

For gold investors, this distinction is significant. A Fed that communicates openly and predictably creates identifiable windows for accumulation and distribution. A Fed that withholds guidance generates structural uncertainty that reshapes how precious metals must be traded.

## The Mechanics of the Warsh Fed: What Has Actually Changed?

### The Dismantling of Forward Guidance

Forward guidance refers to the practice of central banks communicating their future policy intentions to financial markets. Introduced as a standard tool after the Global Financial Crisis, it became central to how bond markets, currency markets, and commodity markets — including gold — were priced through the 2010s and beyond. The relationship between [gold and bond markets](https://discoveryalert.com.au/gold-bonds-dynamics-economic-cycles-2025/) is particularly sensitive to this kind of guidance, as rate signals feed directly into real yield calculations that underpin gold valuations.

> **What is the FOMC Dot Plot?**  
> The dot plot is a chart published by the Federal Reserve showing each policymaker's individual projection for where interest rates will be over coming years. First used in 2012, it became one of the most closely watched forward guidance instruments in global finance, effectively giving markets a visual map of rate expectations across the Committee.

Warsh's decision to withhold his own rate projection from the most recent FOMC dot plot was not a procedural footnote. It was a deliberate signal of institutional philosophy. Credible reports suggest the dot plot itself may be phased out entirely.

The practical consequences of removing this tool are meaningful:

* Rate path uncertainty increases, expanding the volatility premium across interest rate-sensitive asset classes
* Gold and silver pricing shifts from anticipatory to reactive, compressing the forward-looking edge that had previously rewarded disciplined positioning
* Bid-ask spreads widen and short-term price behaviour becomes more erratic as market participants work with less directional information
* The analytical gap between well-resourced institutional traders and retail participants widens

### Internal Fed Restructuring and Data Modernisation

Beyond the guidance question, Warsh has initiated a structural review of the Fed's internal operations, standing up committees focused on tools, systems, and the data infrastructure that underpins monetary decision-making. The stated rationale is that the Fed has historically relied on analytical frameworks and datasets built for a different economic era.

Replacing legacy data systems with real-time analytical infrastructure could, over time, make the Fed's inflation and employment responses faster and more precise. For gold investors, this matters because a more responsive Fed is one that can act earlier in an inflationary cycle, reducing the extended windows of real negative rates that have historically been gold's most fertile environment.

### The Quantitative Easing Contradiction

One of the most analytically interesting tensions inside the Warsh Fed involves quantitative easing. Warsh has been explicit that QE should be a last-resort emergency instrument, not a routine policy lever. His philosophical position is that money supply expansion and inflation are directly linked, and that QE deployed outside genuine crises is inherently inflationary.

However, the Fed's balance sheet expanded by approximately **$10 billion in treasuries** in the most recent reporting period. Open-market treasury purchases are, by functional definition, quantitative easing regardless of the label applied to them.

This contradiction raises a question that gold investors cannot yet answer: Is Warsh genuinely hawkish, or is the current posture a transitional communication strategy designed to anchor inflation expectations before a gradual pivot toward the administration's growth agenda?

## Gold and Silver's Price Response: The Numbers Behind the Correction

### Mapping the 2026 Correction

The market's repricing of Fed expectations under Kevin Warsh Fed and gold prices has been swift and measurable:

| Event | Gold Price Level | Change |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pre-nomination peak | ~$5,500/oz | Baseline |
| Post-nomination (Trump announcement, January 2026) | ~$5,136/oz | -10% |
| Intraday post-announcement low | Below $5,000/oz | -16% from peak |
| Post-June 2026 FOMC (rate hike signal) | ~$4,263/oz | -1.6% single session |
| Mid-2026 trading range | $4,000 to $4,700/oz | Stabilising |

Silver's response amplified the moves seen in gold, consistent with its historically higher volatility coefficient and dual sensitivity to both monetary conditions and industrial demand. This behaviour reflects a well-established pattern: when Fed uncertainty is elevated, silver's beta to risk sentiment accelerates drawdowns relative to gold. Consequently, the [gold-silver ratio](https://discoveryalert.com.au/gold-silver-ratio-analysis-2025-insights-investment/) widened notably during this period, reinforcing the divergence between the two metals under conditions of elevated monetary uncertainty.

Current rate hike probability data offers a real-time sentiment gauge for traders. As of mid-2026, July hike odds remain remote, while September has climbed toward **50%**. These probabilities function as live pricing signals rather than predictions, and their directional shifts correlate closely with short-term gold price movements.

## Two Scenarios and a Framework for Navigating Them

### Scenario A: The Hawk Is Genuine

If Warsh's stated philosophy reflects his actual policy trajectory, the following conditions would likely confirm it:

* No further balance sheet expansion in subsequent reporting periods
* A rate hike materialises by Q3 or Q4 2026
* Inflation data continues softening under tighter conditions

In this scenario, gold faces sustained headwinds, with the **$4,000 support level** subject to meaningful pressure and potential tests of the $3,700 to $3,800 range. Silver would experience deeper percentage drawdowns given its higher sensitivity to risk sentiment.

### Scenario B: The Posture Is Transitional

If Warsh is managing a political balancing act between institutional credibility and administration preferences, the signposts would look different:

* Balance sheet growth continues despite hawkish language
* Rate hikes fail to materialise through H2 2026
* Subsequent FOMC communications soften around the inflation narrative

Under this trajectory, gold would likely recover toward the **$5,000 level** and beyond. JP Morgan's base case places gold at **$6,000 per ounce before 2027**, while Goldman Sachs projects **$4,900 per ounce by December 2026**.

> **Analyst Divergence:** The more than $1,100 gap between Goldman Sachs and JP Morgan's 2026 to 2027 gold price targets is not analytical noise. It reflects genuine uncertainty around Warsh's policy trajectory and underscores why scenario monitoring is more valuable than committing to a point forecast.

### The Signpost Monitoring Framework

Rather than predicting which scenario unfolds, a more disciplined approach involves tracking the indicators that will resolve the uncertainty:

* **Fed balance sheet trajectory**: continued expansion suggests latent accommodative bias regardless of public rhetoric
* **Dot plot survival**: if retained, the distribution of projections across Committee members reveals internal consensus or fracture
* **CPI and PCE trends**: the data inputs Warsh will be forced to respond to publicly
* **Dollar Index (DXY) direction**: the most direct transmission mechanism between Fed policy and gold pricing
* **FOMC dissent patterns**: internal disagreement often precedes policy shifts and can serve as an early pivot signal
* **CME FedWatch rate hike probabilities**: live market-implied probability shifts as a sentiment indicator

## The Structural Implications of an Opaque Fed for Gold Investors

### Volatility as a Long-Run Bullish Variable

The decade of Fed transparency that forward guidance enabled effectively suppressed gold's volatility premium. Predictable policy windows allowed sophisticated investors to time entries and exits with greater precision, which paradoxically dampened the safe-haven premium that makes gold valuable in the first place.

An opaque Fed that withholds guidance and restructures its communication frameworks changes this dynamic. Higher structural volatility in rate expectations expands gold's safe-haven premium over multi-year timeframes. In addition, [central bank gold demand](https://discoveryalert.com.au/central-banks-influencing-gold-prices-2025/) continues to provide a structural floor beneath prices, even as short-term volatility intensifies under the Warsh regime. Investors seeking portfolio insurance against policy uncertainty are willing to pay more for that insurance when uncertainty is genuinely elevated.

### The Inflation Mandate Paradox

There is a scenario worth examining that receives less attention than the straightforward hawkish-is-bearish-for-gold narrative. Aggressive rate hikes that slow economic growth can trigger recessionary fears, which historically redirect capital into gold as a defensive asset. The relationship between Fed hawkishness and gold pricing is not always inverse or linear.

During the Volcker-era tightening cycle of the early 1980s, gold experienced significant volatility but ultimately remained a critical portfolio allocation for investors navigating stagflationary and recessionary uncertainty. The mechanism was different from the inflation-hedge narrative: gold was performing a pure safe-haven function as growth fears overtook inflation concerns.

If Warsh's hawkishness is sufficiently aggressive to generate growth anxiety, a similar dynamic could emerge even within a tightening cycle. The [bond market effects](https://discoveryalert.com.au/trumps-tariff-pause-2025-bond-market-effects/) of this uncertainty are already visible, with yield curve behaviour reflecting genuine disagreement about the growth outlook under tighter monetary conditions.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What did Kevin Warsh do to gold prices in 2026?

Warsh's nomination and subsequent hawkish policy signals triggered a correction of approximately **10 to 16 percent** from peak levels near $5,500 per ounce. By mid-2026, prices had stabilised in the $4,000 to $4,700 range, representing a substantial repricing of the Fed accommodation that had previously been embedded in gold valuations.

### Why does the Fed Chair matter so much to gold prices?

Gold is a non-yielding asset. Its opportunity cost relative to interest-bearing alternatives rises when rates increase and falls when rates decrease. The Fed Chair controls the policy rate trajectory, which feeds directly into real interest rates and US dollar strength — the two most reliable transmission mechanisms to gold pricing.

### What is Kevin Warsh's stance on quantitative easing?

Warsh has publicly positioned QE as an emergency instrument of last resort, opposing its use as a routine policy tool. However, the observed expansion of the Fed's balance sheet through treasury purchases creates a measurable tension between stated philosophy and institutional behaviour.

### Will gold recover if the Fed pivots in late 2026?

Recovery scenarios are supported by both JP Morgan's **$6,000 projection** before 2027 and Goldman Sachs' **$4,900 target** by December 2026. The conditions under which recovery becomes the base case centre on balance sheet behaviour, the materialisation or absence of rate hikes, and shifts in FOMC communication tone. [CNBC's analysis](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/02/02/cnbc-daily-open-gold-and-silver-tank-amid-trump-picking-kevin-warsh-as-fed-chair.html) of the initial market reaction provides useful context for understanding how quickly sentiment can shift around Fed Chair transitions.

### What happened to silver when Warsh became Fed Chair?

Silver sold off faster and more deeply than gold following Warsh's nomination and hawkish positioning. This is consistent with silver's historically higher volatility and its dual exposure to both monetary conditions and industrial demand sentiment. When Fed uncertainty rises, silver's amplified response requires investors to apply a higher risk premium to positioning decisions.

## A Practical Framework for Positioning in the Warsh Era

The most important discipline for precious metals investors navigating the current environment is the separation of Fed language from Fed action. The dynamics underpinning Kevin Warsh Fed and gold prices remain unresolved: Warsh's verbal posture is hawkish, but the balance sheet data tells a more ambiguous story. Until those two signals converge or one definitively overrides the other, committing to a single directional thesis carries unnecessary risk.

The long-term structural case for gold has not changed. Fiscal deficits across major economies remain elevated. Global central bank gold accumulation continues at historically significant rates. De-dollarisation trends, while gradual, are directionally intact. None of these forces have reversed under the Warsh Fed.

What has changed is the short-to-medium-term volatility regime. An opaque Fed that withholds guidance, restructures its internal operations, and sends mixed signals through the gap between rhetoric and balance sheet behaviour is a Fed that demands more disciplined monitoring and more flexible positioning.

> **Final Framework:** Watch the Fed's balance sheet monthly. Track real yields via 10-year TIPS. Monitor DXY direction as the most direct pricing signal. Follow CME FedWatch probability shifts for real-time sentiment. Let the data resolve the scenario uncertainty before committing to directional exposure.

The precious metals market has re-entered an era where monetary policy is the primary variable. That is familiar territory. What is unfamiliar is navigating it without the forward guidance that made Fed positioning legible for the better part of a decade. That is the defining challenge of the Warsh era for gold and silver investors.

This article from Discovery Alert (published July 19, 2026, by Muflih Hidayat) analyzes how Kevin Warsh's appointment as Federal Reserve Chair reshaped the gold market in 2026. The core thesis is that monetary policy has re-established itself as the dominant pricing variable for precious metals after a period (2024-2025) when geopolitical risk, tariffs, and physical demand drove gold with unusual independence from the Fed.

**Key Events:**
- Trump nominated Kevin Warsh to replace Jerome Powell as Fed Chair in early 2026. Markets had priced in a "dovish loyalist," but Warsh proved to be an "institutionally aggressive inflation hawk," triggering the worst single day for gold and silver since the 1980s.
- Gold fell from a pre-nomination peak of ~$5,500/oz to ~$5,136/oz post-nomination (-10%), with an intraday low below $5,000/oz (-16% from peak). After the June 2026 FOMC signaled a rate hike, gold fell to ~$4,263/oz (-1.6% single session). By mid-2026, gold stabilized in a $4,000-$4,700/oz range.
- Market expectations shifted from 1-2 rate cuts in 2026 to pricing in 1-2 rate hikes before year-end. As of mid-2026, September hike odds climbed toward 50%.

**Warsh's Policy Changes:**
- Dismantling of forward guidance: Warsh withheld his own rate projection from the FOMC dot plot (first used in 2012), with reports suggesting it may be phased out entirely. This creates more uncertainty, wider bid-ask spreads, and more volatile short-term price behavior.
- Internal Fed restructuring: Standing up committees focused on tools, systems, and data infrastructure modernization.
- Quantitative easing contradiction: Warsh positions QE as a last-resort emergency instrument, yet the Fed's balance sheet expanded by ~$10 billion in treasuries in the most recent reporting period.

**Two Scenarios:**
- Scenario A (Hawk is genuine): Rate hike materializes by Q3/Q4 2026, no further balance sheet expansion — gold faces pressure at the $4,000 support level, potentially testing $3,700-$3,800.
- Scenario B (Posture is transitional): Rate hikes fail to materialize, balance sheet growth continues — gold recovers toward $5,000+. JP Morgan projects $6,000/oz before 2027; Goldman Sachs projects $4,900/oz by December 2026.

**Monitoring Framework:** Track the Fed balance sheet monthly, 10-year TIPS real yields, DXY dollar direction, CME FedWatch probabilities, CPI/PCE trends, and FOMC dissent patterns.

**Structural Implications:** An opaque Fed increases gold's volatility premium, which paradoxically supports gold's safe-haven value long-term. Central bank gold demand continues to provide a structural floor. Aggressive hiking could trigger recessionary fears that redirect capital into gold (a Volcker-era pattern). The long-term bull case for gold (fiscal deficits, central bank accumulation, de-dollarization) remains intact.

# Kevin Warsh and How the Federal Reserve Impacts the Price of Gold

![Gold bars stacked on top of scattered US dollar bills, signaling wealth and investment](https://cmi-gold-silver.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Blog-images-kevin-warsh-fed-impact-gold-1024x576.png)

The Federal Reserve does not set the price of gold, but it can have an outsized impact on the supply and demand forces that do, at least in the short term. When the Fed raises or lowers interest rates, it changes what investors can earn on cash and bonds, which changes how attractive gold looks by comparison. With Kevin Warsh taking over as Fed chair in May and interest rate policy at its most uncertain point in years, understanding how this relationship works has rarely been more useful. Here’s what the Federal Reserve is, how it operates under its new chairman, and what decades of research say about how its decisions move the price of gold.

## What Is the Federal Reserve?

The Federal Reserve is the central bank of the United States. It manages the country’s financial system primarily by doing three things:

* Controlling the flow of money by purchasing or selling securities like Treasuries
* Lending to large financial institutions when needed to keep the economic gears turning
* Setting short-term interest rates, which affects the cost of borrowing across the entire economy

Congress gave the Fed two goals, often called its dual mandate: keep employment high and keep inflation low. Those goals are frequently in tension. The Fed’s main tool for fighting inflation, raising interest rates, also slows the economy and can cost jobs, which means nearly every Fed decision is a judgment call about which goal needs more attention at that moment.

Interest rate decisions are made by the Federal Open Market Committee, or FOMC, which meets eight times per year and announces whether the federal funds rate will rise, fall, or stay the same. The Fed chair leads that committee, which is why markets react to the chair’s words, sometimes before policy changes at all.

## Who Is Kevin Warsh?

Kevin Warsh took office as chairman of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve on May 22, 2026, for a four-year term, according to the [Federal Reserve](https://www.federalreserve.gov/aboutthefed/bios/board/warsh.htm). This is his second tour at the Fed. He served as a governor from 2006 to 2011, through the financial crisis, before spending more than a decade at Stanford’s Hoover Institution and as a partner at Duquesne Family Office. Earlier in his career he worked at Morgan Stanley and served as an economic policy advisor in the White House.

Warsh has chosen to say less publicly than his predecessors, which puts a premium on the words he does use. [CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/07/22/kevin-warsh-has-homed-in-on-three-key-phrases-how-fed-watchers-interpret-them.html) counted three phrases across his first five public appearances: “family fight” 13 times, “first principles” 11 times, and “inflation is a choice” six times.

Claudia Sahm, chief economist at New Century Advisors, told CNBC that “‘first principles’ is code for ‘question everything.'” Mark Spindel, chief investment officer at Potomac River Capital, said the “family fight” phrase describes the natural debate inside the FOMC, but also functions as a shield: “It’s also a way of deflecting his responsibility from external pressure.”

“Inflation is a choice” is the phrase gold investors should watch most closely. It’s a nod to Warsh’s mentor Milton Friedman, who famously said that inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon, and Fed watchers broadly read it as Warsh holding the Fed itself accountable for bringing inflation down. Markets have translated that into one word: hawkish.

## How Does the Federal Reserve Impact Gold Prices?

The Fed cannot directly change the value of gold, but its decisions ripple through the two things that price gold every day: the dollar and interest rates. Gold is priced in dollars and pays no interest, so anything that strengthens the dollar or raises the return on cash and bonds changes gold’s appeal.

### What happens to gold when the Fed raises rates?

When the Fed raises the federal funds rate, borrowing gets more expensive, but savings accounts, CDs, and Treasury bonds start paying more. Gold offers no dividend or interest. Its only return comes from price appreciation, which means that when interest-bearing investments are paying well, they tend to be favored over gold, and gold’s price can dip. This is the dynamic that defined June 2026, when rate-hike expectations under Warsh’s new Fed pushed gold to its worst quarter in 13 years and briefly below $4,000 an ounce, which we covered in our [June spot price recap.](https://cmi-gold-silver.com/article/june-2026-spot-price-recap/)

### What happens to gold when the Fed cuts rates?

The reverse. Cash and bonds pay less, so holding gold costs investors less in forgone interest. Rate cuts also frequently signal that the Fed is worried about the economy, which is historically when gold has done well as a store of wealth.

### So does the Fed have direct control over gold prices?

Not exactly. Inflation, economic uncertainty, and global demand are the primary drivers of gold, and Fed policy works on gold through those channels rather than around them. Gold isn’t guaranteed to fall just because the Fed hikes, and it isn’t guaranteed to rally just because the Fed cuts. What the Fed reliably changes is the opportunity cost of holding gold, and over time, that cost is one of the most powerful forces in the market.

### What the Research Says

The Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago published one of the most thorough studies on this question, [examining what has driven gold prices](https://www.chicagofed.org/-/media/publications/chicago-fed-letter/2021/cfl464-pdf.pdf) across five decades of data. Its economists tested the three most common claims about gold, that it hedges inflation, that it responds to real interest rates, and that it protects against bad economic times, and found meaningful support for all three:

* A one percentage point rise in the long-term real interest rate lowers the real price of gold by 13.1%
* An extra percentage point of ten-year expected inflation raises the real price of gold by 37%, which the researchers noted is “well in line with the long-held ‘inflation hedge’ view”
* A one standard deviation increase in the share of consumers expecting bad economic times raises the gold price by 9.7%

[Chicago Fed](https://www.chicagofed.org/-/media/publications/chicago-fed-letter/2021/cfl464-pdf.pdf)

[Chicago Fed](https://www.chicagofed.org/-/media/publications/chicago-fed-letter/2021/cfl464-pdf.pdf)

Notice that real interest rates\* and inflation expectations push in opposite directions, which explains a lot about 2026. Inflation is elevated, which supports gold, but the Fed’s response to it, higher rates, works against gold at the same time. The result is the tug-of-war investors have been living through since February.

There’s also a longer-run force underneath the rate cycle. A [2024 study in the European Financial and Accounting Journal](https://www.econstor.eu/bitstream/10419/315553/1/1921999608.pdf) found that the price of gold and the U.S. M2 money supply\* have moved together for over 50 years. When gold has strayed far from that relationship, it has always come back, though not quickly: the overvaluation of 1980 took ten years to correct, the 2007 overvaluation took seven, and the undervaluation of 2001 took six years to close. The money supply grows under every Fed chair, hawkish or dovish, which is a large part of why gold’s long-term trajectory has survived all of them.

[Econstor](https://www.econstor.eu/bitstream/10419/315553/1/1921999608.pdf)

## What This Means for Gold Investors

If the Fed hikes and inflation cools, the opportunity cost of holding gold stays high and prices likely stay under pressure. If inflation stays sticky despite higher rates, or the economy weakens under them, the Chicago Fed’s research suggests gold benefits from both the inflation channel and the bad-times channel at once. [Reuters reported](https://www.reuters.com/world/india/gold-slips-fading-us-iran-peace-prospects-reinforce-fed-rate-hike-bets-2026-07-01/) in early July that fading U.S.-Iran peace prospects and elevated oil prices were reinforcing rate-hike bets, with markets pricing roughly a 67% chance of a September hike heading into Warsh’s first FOMC meeting as chair.  
 In the long term, the forces that matter most don’t depend on who chairs the Fed. The money supply keeps growing, central banks keep buying, and government debt keeps rising. We’ve written about how these forces played out in real time, including [why gold didn’t rally when the Iran war began](https://cmi-gold-silver.com/why-arent-gold-and-silver-rallying/) and [what gold is signaling about inflation](https://cmi-gold-silver.com/are-gold-and-silver-sending-a-warning-about-inflation-instead-of-war/).

If you’re considering adding physical gold to your portfolio, [check our daily spot prices](https://www.cmi-gold-silver.com/gold-silver-daily-spot-prices) or [learn more about getting started.](https://www.cmi-gold-silver.com/buying-gold/)

***\*Real interest rates are interest rates adjusted for inflation, showing the true return investors earn after accounting for rising prices.***

***\*M2 money supply is a broad measure of money in the U.S. economy that includes cash, checking deposits, savings accounts, small-time deposits, and retail money market funds.***

The Federal Reserve has battled a variety of economic troubles over the past 35 years. Between tech busts, a financial crisis and a pandemic, not to mention periods of too little inflation and too much, the nation’s central bank has used short-term interest rates, along with other more novel measures, to fulfill its reason for being: Keep prices stable and maximize unemployment.

As the Fed currently endeavors to wind down inflation without causing a recession, it is useful to see how and why it acted in the past.

Forbes Advisor has compiled this history as a handy guide to the course of the federal funds rate and the Federal Reserve’s monetary policy decisions since 1990.

## Understanding Fed Interest Rate Decisions

The federal funds rate is the main lever the Federal Reserve uses to manage the economy.

In keeping with its mandate, the Fed prefers inflation to be 2% and for the labor market to be as fully employed as possible without causing inflation to go beyond that target rate.

Should prices rise too slowly (like in the 2010s), the Fed will lower rates to spur economic growth. The theory is that lower rates incentivize more economic activity because banks are more likely to lend cash than let it sit on the sidelines earning meager returns.

Conversely, when prices rise too quickly (like in the aftermath of the pandemic), the Fed will raise rates in order to stymie economic activity. The unemployment rate will tend to rise (as has happened over the past year or so), as businesses find it harder to invest.

The Fed, though, doesn’t just rely on inflation and employment metrics to devise its monetary policy. It considers all sorts of indicators, from housing starts to consumer spending, to gauge just how well the economy is performing.

It will act quickly in the face of unforeseen events, such as a global pandemic or terrorist attack.

While Congress holds the purse strings, market participants look to how and why the Fed acts when placing their bets on the future.

### About the Data

The tables below list the dates of Fed meetings when the Federal Open Market Committee changed interest rates, the size of each rate change in basis points—abbreviated as bps—and the resulting federal funds target rate range.

Basis points are a common unit of measurement for interest rates. One basis point is equal to 1/100 th of one percentage point, or 0.01%. For instance, a half a percentage point change in an interest rate would equal 50 basis points.

Please note that before 1990, the Fed didn’t explicitly target a set federal funds rate. If you’re interested in earlier rate policy, look through this [Federal Reserve document](https://www.federalreserve.gov/foia/files/20190829-changes-intended-federal-funds-rate.pdf) produced through a Freedom of Information Act request.

## Fed Rate Cuts 2024-2026: Still Taming Inflation

The Federal Reserve kept its benchmark interest rate unchanged at 3.50%to 3.75% following the July Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC)meeting.In a shift from June’s meeting,where the vote was unanimous, three out of 12 committee members voted against the monetary action, preferring to raise the target rate by a quarter percentage point.

The new Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, echoed his stance from June’s meeting.Warsh refrained from offering his own forward projection and stated that his lack of estimations could have contributed to the higher nominal and real yields across the Treasury curve in the bond market.The statement presumes that the market relied on real data and investor actions to price government bonds instead of using his projection to influence their decisions.

“Market participants are learning to play ball, not referee,and market prices will continue to respond in the direction and magnitude they see fit,”said Warsh.Overall, Warsh said the economy is showing impressive resilience, despite recent shocks.

JPMorgan forecasts GDP growth of 1.5% to 2.0% amid rising inflation if spending is resilient,AI capital expenditures remain robust and conflicts in the Middle East progress toward resolution.Expectations for future Federal Reserve rate hikes have grown amid rising headline inflation.

“Inflation remains elevated relative to the Committee’s 2%goal, in part reflecting supply shocks that have driven price increases in certain sectors, including energy,” according to the FOMC’s July news release.

Middle Eastern conflicts are complicating matters for the Fed, with soaring oil and gas prices. Higher energy prices could have a ripple effect on other costs, like food and utilities.

The predictions market is pricing in at least one rate hike before year-end.

### 2024-2025

In 2025, there were three consecutive 25-basis-point rate cuts: one at the September FOMC meeting, another at the October meeting, and a third in December.

# Gold holds steady ahead of Fed's rate decision

[WATCH LIVE](/live-tv/)

In this article

* [XAU=](/quotes/XAU=)
* [@GC.1](/quotes/@GC.1)
* [XAG=](/quotes/XAG=)

Gold prices were largely steady on Wednesday as investors awaited the U.S. Federal Reserve's policy decision and comments from Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh for clues on inflation and interest rate outlooks.

Alexander Manzyuk | Anadolu Agency | Getty Images

Gold prices were largely steady on Wednesday as investors awaited the [U.S. Federal Reserve's](https://www.cnbc.com/federal-reserve/) policy decision and comments from Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh for clues on inflation and interest rate outlooks.

[Spot gold](/quotes/XAU=/) was little changed at $4,029.08 per ounce by 0301 GMT. [U.S. gold futures](/quotes/@GC.1/) for August delivery dipped 0.2% to $4,028.10.

"Gold is very much connected to today's FOMC meeting.... The scenario that may see a potential reversal of the recent bearish bias in gold prices will be the Fed turning to a less hawkish rhetoric," said Kelvin Wong, a senior market analyst at OANDA.

The Fed's policy decision is due at 1800 GMT, while Kevin Warsh's comments are scheduled for 1830 GMT.

Market expectations indicate a 70% chance that the central bank will hold rates steady and a 30% probability of a 25 basis points hike, according to the FedWatch tool. Markets are pricing in a 76% chance of an increase in September.

Meanwhile, the Bank of England and the Bank of Japan are widely expected to keep rates unchanged on Thursday and Friday, respectively, and caution against rising inflation.

Gold is seen as a hedge against inflation, and higher rates increase the opportunity cost of holding the non-yielding metal.

On the geopolitical front, the U.S. military said on Tuesday it intercepted multiple ballistic missiles launched by Iran towards U.S. forces in the Middle East in what Washington cast as "an attempted surprise attack" by Tehran.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards later said they fired several ballistic missiles at a U.S. air base and a U.S. military Central Command center in Jordan.

Oil prices drifted higher, supported by shrinking U.S. crude inventories.

Commerzbank on Tuesday lowered its year-end gold price forecast to $4,500 per troy ounce and said it expects silver to reach $67 per troy ounce by the end of the year.

[Spot silver](/quotes/XAG=/) gained 0.9% to $57.65 per ounce and [platinum](/quotes/XPT=/) inched 0.3% higher to $1,600.40. [Palladium](https://www.cnbc.com/palladium/) fell 0.7% to $1,261.

This article from CanadianMiningReport.com (authored by Ben McGregor, July 3, 2026) provides a gold price prediction for July 2026, presenting both the bull case and bear case.

**Current Context:** After a sharp correction from all-time highs near $5,500–$5,600 per ounce in January 2026, gold stabilized and traded around $4,100–$4,190 in early July 2026. Recent weaker-than-expected U.S. non-farm payrolls data reduced near-term Federal Reserve rate-hike expectations, providing a tailwind for gold. Major bank year-end 2026 forecasts remain constructive, with targets ranging from ~$4,900 (Goldman Sachs) to $6,000+ (J.P. Morgan and others).

**Bull Case:** Key drivers include softer economic data providing Fed flexibility (lower real yields reduce holding costs), ongoing central bank/structural demand and safe-haven buying amid geopolitical uncertainty and fiscal concerns, technical/sentiment recovery after the correction (stabilization above ~$4,000), and broader precious metals strength. Constructive scenario: gold could test/ exceed $4,200–$4,500+ during July.

**Bear Case:** Risks include resilient economic data and hawkish policy re-emerging, dollar strength and higher Treasury yields increasing gold's opportunity cost, profit-taking and technical resistance, reduced ETF inflows, and geopolitical de-escalation reducing safe-haven demand. Downside scenario could see retests near $4,000 or below.

**Mining Stock Implications:** Higher/stable gold prices expand margins for low-AISC producers with strong balance sheets and Tier-1 jurisdictions; junior developers may see improved financing. Prolonged weakness would pressure higher-cost producers, shifting focus to companies with strong balance sheets, hedging, or diversification. Sector equities amplify metal price moves in both directions.

**Conclusion:** The near-term picture leans constructively with stabilization and rebound potential, while structural drivers (central bank buying, long-term investors) support a longer-term bullish bias. July outcomes hinge on U.S. economic data and Fed expectations. The article includes a disclaimer noting it is educational, not investment advice, and that gold/mining equities are highly volatile.

# Gold Price Falls Below US$4,000, How Low Can it Go?

![]()

[Written by Charlotte McLeod](https://investingnews.com/author/charlotte-mcleod/)

|

Jun. 24, 2026 10:30AM PST

After a record-setting run earlier this year, the gold price dipped below US$4,000. Experts weigh in on where the metal could go from here.

**Gold is feeling the summer heat with a drop below US$4,000 per ounce on Wednesday (June 24).**

The yellow metal hasn't been below that key psychological level since November 2025, but a stronger US dollar, expectations of higher [interest rates](https://investingnews.com/us-federal-reserve-interest-rates/) and cooling tensions in the Middle East are combining to push the price down.

---

![Gold price chart, November 2025 to June 2026.](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%201990%20700'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

*Gold price chart, November 2025 to June 2026.*

*Chart via the [Investing News Network](https://investingnews.com/gold-price-chart/).*

The decline comes after a record-setting run that took gold to [an all-time high](https://investingnews.com/daily/resource-investing/precious-metals-investing/gold-investing/highest-price-for-gold/) of US$5,589.38 in January of this year. While a correction from that level was widely expected, experts are divided on what's next.

Let's take a look at three potential price scenarios for gold moving forward: bear, neutral and bull.

### Bear scenario: Gold price falls to US$3,500

In an interview at the end of April, [Gareth Soloway of VerifiedInvesting.com](https://investingnews.com/gareth-soloway-gold-update/) said he thought gold would likely come down to US$4,300, and after that could potentially continue falling.

"The chart's telling me that we're likely coming down to this US$4,300 level, maybe a small bounce, then we'll break down to US$3,900 here," he said. "Now again, will that be the bottom in gold or not? That's a good question. I do think that there's potential for a washout later this year, back to about the US$3,500 level."

Soloway's [gold price](https://investingnews.com/gold-price-chart/) target is based on technical analysis, but [Chris Temple of the National Investor](https://investingnews.com/chris-temple-gold-uranium-forecast/) has identified a variety of fundamental reasons that could take gold as low as US$3,500. The main one is that he thinks the US Federal Reserve is no longer in a position to cut interest rates in the near term.

"Bottom line, in my view, what causes gold to turn around is when the Fed has to stop pretending that it cares about inflation, that it can do a darn thing about it, and just starts going nuts," he said.

"That's when gold gets going again, and we're a little ways from that."

### Neutral scenario: Gold price trades sideways

Both Soloway and Temple are positive on gold long term, meaning they see higher prices after a deeper correction — in fact, Soloway emphasized that if the metal does fall to US$3,500, he would be buying long-term positions.

The same can be said for the experts who anticipate more sideways movement from gold over the summer — after further consolidation in the summer months they're calling for higher prices.

In a late May interview, [Ronald-Peter Stoeferle of Incrementum](https://investingnews.com/ronald-peter-stoeferle-gold-forecast/) and the "In Gold We Trust" report said that at the moment gold lacks immediate catalysts, commenting, "We're seeing some headwinds, we're seeing very weak seasonality, we're already seeing ... lots of negative sentiment in the market, especially in the gold and silver miners."

Stoeferle added, "I wouldn't expect too much for gold and silver over the next couple of weeks, probably after the World Cup is done, I think. Then perhaps there's going to be more upside — but that's just correlation, not causation."

Stoeferle's ultimate target for gold in this cycle is US$8,900; on a seasonal basis, he noted that historically either the end of July or the beginning of August tends to be the bottom for the metal, as well as the miners.

### Bull scenario: Gold price rises to US$8,900

But what about a more immediately bullish scenario for gold?

The best place to find that is with [David Hunter of Contrarian Macro Advisors](https://investingnews.com/david-hunter-gold-silver-forecast/). At the beginning of May, he said he anticipates a major breakout in gold and silver — and he doesn't think it will take long:

> "We should see a pretty fast run, meaning over the next few months — three, four or five months — with silver going from the mid-US$70s here up to US$180, and gold going from where it is now up to US$6,800. Post-bust, gold can get to US$20,000, as I said, and silver can get to US$1,000.

> "I thought US$500 was going to be kind of a crazy number (for silver), and after seeing what we've seen this year, I had to raise it. And I think silver at US$1,000 may sound crazy, but I think that's very doable for, you know, early next decade."

It's worth clarifying what Hunter means when he talks about a bust — although he sees gold and silver moving much higher in the near term, after that he's calling for a global bust.

It's not until after that bust that he expects his US$20,000 gold and US$1,000 silver targets.

### Are big banks still bullish on gold?

While gold market participants clearly remain bullish in the long term, what do those outside the sector think?

[Goldman Sachs (NYSE:GS)](https://investingnews.com/stocks/gs/the-goldman-sachs-grou/) made headlines earlier this month when it cut its 2026 year-end gold price call [from US$5,400 to US$4,900](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-06-19/goldman-sachs-lops-500-off-gold-target-on-no-fed-cuts-this-year). The firm said the reduction is based on the expectation that the Fed won't cut rates this year — it's anticipating lower inflows into gold exchange-traded funds as a result.

"Our gold price views remain structurally constructive but tactically cautious, with near-term downside risk and medium-term upside risk," analysts Lina Thomas and Daan Struyven wrote.

In the event that the Fed hikes rates in 2026, they believe gold could fall to US$4,400 by the end of the year.

[Deutsche Bank (NYSE:DB)](https://investingnews.com/stocks/db/deutsche-bank/) also recently [lowered its gold price outlook](https://ca.finance.yahoo.com/news/deutsche-bank-cuts-gold-outlook-110408669.html), saying it's forecasting US$4,800 in the fourth quarter. The firm was [previously looking for US$6,000](https://www.cnbc.com/video/2026/02/02/deutsche-bank-reiterates-6000oz-gold-target-despite-heavy-selling.html).

However, [other big banks](https://goldsilver.com/industry-news/goldsilver-news/goldman-sachs-gold-target-cut-jpmorgan-divergence/) have left much higher gold price predictions intact.

[Wells Fargo & Co. (NYSE:WFC)](https://investingnews.com/stocks/nyse-wfc/wells-fargo-company/) has so far retained its [March call of US$6,100 to US$6,300](https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/commodities/articles/wells-fargo-resets-gold-price-153300506.html), and [JPMorgan Chase & Co. (NYSE:JPM)](https://investingnews.com/stocks/jpm/jpmorgan-chase-co/) is standing firm with a [June outlook of US$6,000](https://www.jpmorgan.com/insights/global-research/commodities/gold-prices).

Whether the summer months bring changes remains to be seen. At this point, a key takeaway is that even banks that have lowered their expectations for gold still see the price going higher than it is today.

This article from the Investing News Network (written by Charlotte McLeod, published June 24, 2026) reports on gold's price dropping below US$4,000 per ounce on Wednesday, June 24, 2026 — the first time below that key psychological level since November 2025. The decline follows a record-setting run that took gold to an all-time high of US$5,589.38 in January 2026. Factors pushing the price down include a stronger US dollar, expectations of higher interest rates, and cooling tensions in the Middle East.

The article presents three expert price scenarios for gold:

**Bear scenario (US$3,500):** Gareth Soloway of VerifiedInvesting.com predicts, based on technical analysis, gold could fall to US$4,300, bounce, then break down to US$3,900, with potential for a washout to around US$3,500 later this year. Chris Temple of the National Investor also sees potential for gold to fall as low as US$3,500 for fundamental reasons, primarily that the US Federal Reserve is no longer in a position to cut interest rates in the near term.

**Neutral scenario (sideways trading):** Ronald-Peter Stoeferle of Incrementum ('In Gold We Trust' report) sees gold lacking immediate catalysts, with weak seasonality and negative market sentiment. He expects little movement over the next few weeks, potentially until after the World Cup. On a seasonal basis, he notes the end of July or beginning of August historically tends to be the bottom for gold and miners. His ultimate cycle target is US$8,900.

**Bull scenario (US$8,900 or higher):** David Hunter of Contrarian Macro Advisors anticipates a major breakout within the next 3-5 months, with gold rising to US$6,800 and silver from mid-US$70s to US$180. After a predicted global bust, he sees gold reaching US$20,000 and silver US$1,000 by early next decade.

**Big bank outlooks:** Goldman Sachs cut its 2026 year-end gold price call from US$5,400 to US$4,900, citing expectations that the Fed won't cut rates this year (anticipating lower ETF inflows). They noted if the Fed hikes rates in 2026, gold could fall to US$4,400 by year-end. Deutsche Bank lowered its outlook to US$4,800 for Q4 (previously US$6,000). However, Wells Fargo retained its March call of US$6,100-6,300, and JPMorgan Chase stands firm with a June outlook of US$6,000. A key takeaway: even banks that lowered expectations still see gold going higher than current prices.

The article notes that both Soloway and Temple see higher long-term prices after a deeper correction, and Soloway indicated he would buy long-term positions if gold falls to US$3,500.

# Why Is the Gold Price Falling? Drivers of the 2026 Correction

Spot gold traded near $4,100 per ounce on 11 June 2026, after an intraday print of $4,023.95 — the weakest level since November 2025 — and roughly 26% below the record of $5,595 set on 29 January, leaving the metal negative for the year. For a treasury, family office, or reserve manager carrying allocated bullion, the operative question is which layer of demand repriced. On the published flow data, the official-sector bid that anchored the 2025–26 advance has not moved: central banks stayed net buyers through the drawdown, at a pace above their five-year average. The repricing happened in the financial layer above it — Federal Reserve expectations, real yields, the dollar, and fund positioning — reset by the early-June data within a single trading week. Each driver below carries a date and a named source; where sources weight the causes differently, the difference is stated rather than averaged.

## What the 2026 Correction Has Done

Gold rose more than 65% over 2025 and extended the advance into the new year, reaching a record $5,595 per ounce on 29 January. A drawdown in March gave way to sideways trade inside a band capped near $4,800, and May closed about 1% lower. The break came in the second week of June, compressed into four sessions:

| Date (2026) | Event | Indicative level, USD/oz |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 29 Jan | Record print after the January advance | $5,595 |
| 5 Jun | May payrolls above consensus; unemployment steady at 4.3%, prior two months revised up a combined 93,000; markets re-priced toward a possible Fed hike | Down more than 3% on the session — the steepest one-day drop in weeks; the year’s advance erased |
| 8 Jun | Follow-through selling | $4,289.9 — a two-month low; $4,268.5 intraday |
| 10 Jun | May CPI: 4.2% y/y headline (+0.5% m/m), core 2.9% | Brief recovery after the print, lower into the close |
| 11 Jun | Extension of the slide, then a partial rebound | $4,105 last; $4,023.95 intraday — the lowest print since November 2025 |

*Levels are indicative prints from the reporting listed under Sources; not executable quotes.*

The 5 June session removed the year’s gain; the sessions that followed took the metal under its 1 January line, and gold stands negative for the year as of 11 June. The move runs across the precious complex: silver, which set its own record early in the year, trades near $67. For valuation work, the reference window is the operative variable — a mark, mandate trigger, or collateral haircut keyed to a January level sits roughly a quarter above the current print, and a repricing of this speed shortens the interval over which any quoted figure stays usable.

## The Reserve-Asset Bid: What Has Not Moved

Through the drawdown, the published official-sector record shows continuity. For Q1 2026, the World Gold Council (WGC) — the industry body whose statistics on central-bank and fund gold demand serve as the market’s reference series — estimates net additions of 244 tonnes, above the prior quarter and above the five-year average. Behind that quarter sits an elevated base: net purchases reached about 863 tonnes in 2025, roughly double the pre-2022 norm of 400–500 tonnes a year, and projections for 2026 — from J.P. Morgan’s commodities research, the WGC, and asset manager State Street — cluster in a 750–850 tonne range.

Month by month, the texture is uneven — and the unevenness is informative. At 5 tonnes, January net purchases ran far below the trailing twelve-month average of 27; the pause coincided with the record print, and a higher price level mechanically slows incremental accumulation. By April, buying had resumed, with the National Bank of Poland adding 14 tonnes. An institution running a fixed reserve-share target converts a price move into a quantity adjustment and keeps acquiring across price levels — the purchase decision sits in policy, and a weekly drawdown does not reach it.

The buyer base has also broadened. Institutions absent from the market for years, or never present, have entered — among recent buyers, the central banks of Guatemala, Indonesia, and Malaysia; the Bank of Korea is adding gold exposure to its reserve portfolio from Q1 2026, its first gold-related step since 2013. In the WGC’s most recent reserve survey, 95% of responding central banks expected global official gold holdings to rise over the following twelve months. Reported selling stays concentrated in a small number of institutions managing domestic fiscal pressures.

A more cautious reading comes from Citi: the commodities research team at US bank Citigroup lists moderating central-bank demand, alongside ETF flows, among the reasons its June note trimmed near-term expectations. The two readings differ in window length — the monthly pace did slow in January; the quarterly aggregate still cleared the five-year average. Operationally, what matters is the nature of this bid: policy-driven and price-inelastic. It sets physical offtake over quarters and defends no price level inside a trading week — which is how a drawdown of a quarter from the record coexists with above-average official buying, and why this is the demand layer institutions point to when holding [gold as a strategic reserve asset](https://goldenarkreserve.com/blog/gold-strategic-reserve-asset/). The layers that repriced are the ones marked daily: rate expectations, the dollar, and fund positioning.

## Rate Repricing: The Main Engine of the Decline

Until the first week of June, the carry argument for gold rested on an easing path. Two data prints removed it. The 5 June payroll report showed a labor market resilient enough that markets began re-betting on the possibility of a rate hike — pricing shifted from the timing of a cut to the odds of the opposite move. The 10 June CPI confirmed the constraint: inflation at 4.2% keeps the Federal Reserve restrictive and lifts real Treasury yields, and higher real yields raise the cost of holding a non-yielding asset. Named desks now price that constraint directly into their gold view: the French banking group BNP Paribas expects the Fed to begin raising rates in December and to continue in the following months, and Bart Melek, head of global commodity strategy at TD Securities, notes that with employment strong and inflation pressure significant, the Fed has virtually no inclination to cut — the opportunity cost of holding gold keeps rising. The WGC’s June market commentary works from the same premise: the Fed may need to hike as inflation pressures mount.

The mechanism is arithmetic, not sentiment. Bullion pays no coupon, so every holder finances the position against the real yield available elsewhere; when the expected policy path swings from cuts to a possible hike, that comparison moves against gold at every horizon simultaneously. The holder this reaches first is the financial one — the fund or treasury marking the position daily against bills, whose hurdle rate moved inside a single week. The policy-driven reserve buyer of the previous section runs no such mark, which is why one layer sold and the other did not.

Compounding the move, the dollar index has pushed through the 100 mark, firming alongside yields; a dollar-priced metal in a strengthening dollar costs more in every other settlement currency, thinning the price-sensitive physical demand that the ETF and regional flow figures record. The 16–17 June policy meeting is the next point at which this entire pricing gets re-tested; any figure quoted in the current tape carries a short shelf life into it.

## Energy Prices and the Inflation Channel

At 4.2% headline against 2.9% core, the May CPI shows where the damage sits: 1.3 percentage points of headline inflation in the volatile components, with energy the largest of them. Once crude moved above $112 a barrel, the macro backdrop turned dollar-positive — elevated energy prices fed the inflation prints and global-inflation concerns, cut expectations of lower rates, and kept the Fed restrictive, a configuration that works directly against gold. Gold’s usual inflation-hedge reflex fails against this kind of print, because the policy response to energy-led inflation is tighter money, and the rates channel dominates.

Inside the same fortnight, the energy input has cut against gold from both directions. Elevated crude pressed the price through the rates channel above. Then the reversal pressed it again: on 9 June the crude benchmarks gave back two weeks of gains in a session — WTI down about 4% to $87.6, Brent at $90.9 — and the supply-risk premium that had supported both barrels and bullion came out together; Citi listed weakening safe-haven premiums among the conditions behind its June reassessment. A position that loses on the spike through rates and loses on the retreat through premium decay has no stable energy-price scenario working for it in the current configuration — which is the precise answer to why the decline has run through both phases of the oil move.

What remains open is duration. The WGC expects the headwind could persist for as long as the energy-supply disruption does; the policy response to the inflation it generates is equally unsettled. Both questions close on events, and neither event carries a date.

## Investment Flows: ETFs, Futures Positioning, and Physical Demand

As of the latest published record — data through 31 May — the fund layer shows the retreat in dated, audited numbers; the June break itself has not yet reached print. In May, global physically backed gold ETFs shed a net US$2bn, with Europe the only region to register inflows: European funds drew US$334mn while Asia (−US$1.2bn) and North America (−US$1.1bn) led the outflows. Regional texture is specific. Asia’s first monthly outflow since August 2025 traces almost entirely to China — softer local gold prices, renminbi appreciation, and a strong equity tape pulling allocation — while India posted US$610mn of redemptions, ending twelve consecutive months of inflows, with most of the selling following the announcement of higher import tariffs. Policy inputs, not the dollar price alone, are moving the price-sensitive book.

On the stock side the picture differs from the flow side, and the distinction matters for reading the episode. Total ETF assets fell 2% in the month to US$604bn — mostly a price effect — while collective holdings eased just 0.4% to 4,121 tonnes, barely below the record 4,176 tonnes set on 27 February 2026; year-to-date net flows remain positive at nearly US$17bn. The financial holder has stepped to the sidelines at the margin; it has not liquidated the stock. The WGC’s own read is of investors sidelined by rangebound prices and renewed risk appetite, with technology ETFs booking their largest single-month intake since the start of 2024 — and the opportunity cost of holding gold rising on dollar strength and higher rates, against a re-set expected rate path: the same arithmetic already moving every daily-marked book.

From the leveraged layer, little signal: COMEX managed-money positioning sat in neutral territory through May, a modest US$1.4bn (8t) gain, and the WGC’s attribution model found no standout driver among its explicit variables — flagging that part of the move may sit in over-the-counter flows the model does not capture. A neutral futures book into the June break means the slide was not primarily a forced unwind of stretched longs — and leaves correspondingly less forced selling to exhaust. Citi’s note adds the physical margin: central-bank and ETF demand moderating together took steam out of the rally, and its analysts flag weak physical demand as a continuing pressure point.

What can be verified today is therefore partial. Holdings sit within half a percent of their record and trading volumes run slightly above the 2025 average; flows have stalled while year-to-date totals stay positive, and positioning shows no stretch to unwind. Whether June turned the stall into liquidation is what the next monthly prints will establish — they land in early July, and until then the flow side of this episode rests on a one-month evidence lag.

## Where Analyst Explanations Agree — and Where They Split

On the proximate cause there is no real dispute: the early-June data reset the policy path, and real yields and the dollar carried the move. Citi’s 8 June note attributes its reassessment to stabilizing real yields, a stronger short-term dollar bias, weakening safe-haven premiums, and a less supportive demand backdrop — “limited catalysts for a sustained move higher in the very near term” — and analysts led by Kenny Hu see weak physical demand compounding the pressure if the energy-supply disruption runs through the end of summer. The rate-path desks quoted earlier — TD Securities on rising opportunity cost, BNP Paribas on hikes resuming — sit in the same camp.

DataTrek Research, an independent New York market-research firm, locates the cause in the speed and scale of the earlier rally: co-founders Nicholas Colas and Jessica Rabe explain the weakness simply — the metal “rallied too far, too fast” through 2025 and into the new year. On that account, the same payroll and inflation prints would have produced a smaller move against a slower run-up; the data were the trigger, the speed was the cause.

Goldman Sachs supplies a third, mechanical account. Analysts at the US investment bank point to gold’s depth itself: high liquidity makes the metal a natural source of cash when investors face liquidity needs, for instance in an equity sell-off amid higher rates and weaker growth expectations. Selling of that kind carries no view on gold — and it stops when the liquidity need stops, independent of anything in the gold market.

The measurement position belongs to the WGC: its attribution model found no standout driver in May, with modest drags from risk sentiment and Asian and US ETF outflows and a residual possibly sitting in OTC flows outside the model — an honest statement that part of the selling is visible only by subtraction. The one genuine data dispute remains the official-sector read, and it is a dispute about window length, not about the numbers: monthly pace slowed in January; the quarterly aggregate cleared the five-year average. Each explanation also nominates its own test — the rates account is re-examined at every inflation print and at the 16–17 June meeting, the liquidity account by whether selling abates when equity and funding stress does, the speed account by whether the price stabilises with no macro change at all. Several banks revised their gold views during the June repricing; the current set of [bank targets 2026–2027](https://goldenarkreserve.com/insights/gold-price-forecast-2026-2027/) is maintained on a dedicated reference page.

## What a Falling Reference Price Means at Transaction Level

In a week of 3% sessions, the distance between a published price and a dealable one stops being routine and becomes the operative number. Published gold prices — this episode’s prints included — are reference figures: delayed, rounded, and aggregated from third-party market data, the same basis on which a [live indicative gold price reference](https://goldenarkreserve.com/gold-price/) is maintained. An executable level exists only inside a live quote, and a quote specifies format, quantity, location, and settlement window. Screen prints update continuously, while dealable quotes arrive with shortened validity and re-quote more often — the screen establishes direction, the quote establishes the level a transaction clears at.

Transmission into dealing terms runs through three components, each on its own schedule. With volatility, the dealing spread around the reference widens, because the quoting counterparty carries the price risk between quote and acceptance. The format premium responds to physical supply and demand in a specific bar class — fabrication, logistics, availability — and does not track the spot print one-for-one: a lower reference does not cut the all-in acquisition figure by the same amount if the premium firms. And the settlement window prices time itself. The longer the interval between instruction and settlement, the more reference-price variance the parties sit through — with inflation release dates and the 16–17 June policy meeting now functioning as scheduled repricing points. Comparable offers are therefore all-in figures for an identical format, location, and settlement window; a bare per-ounce number compares nothing.

Execution records outlast the move. A transaction record fixes price, date, and format at execution; the same record carries the serial numbers and the settlement evidence. What a treasury, auditor, or mandate review reads later is that record against the then-current reference — the difference between the two is the realized position, whatever the screen did in between. A repricing of this speed is exactly what that fixing exists for: a position documented at execution reconciles; a position referenced to “the gold price” as a single undated number does not.

On the way out, the same mechanics run in mirror. A falling reference reaches a seller through the bid side of the same spread, and through the format’s standing in the secondary market: bars in LBMA-recognised refinery formats with continuous documentation re-enter the professional chain without re-assay and carry the narrowest exit spreads, so the cost of the round trip is largely set at acquisition — in the format and records chosen — and only realized at exit. Where this episode sits within a longer holding rationale is a question of [institutional allocation context](https://goldenarkreserve.com/invest-in-gold/) — the layer that kept buying against the layers that repriced.

## Gold Price Crash of June 2026 — Drivers and Analysis

This article from Golden Ark Reserve examines why gold prices fell sharply in June 2026, analyzing the correction from an institutional/reserve-manager perspective.

### Timeline of the Correction
- **29 January 2026**: Gold reached a record **$5,595/oz** after rising more than 65% over 2025.
- **5 June 2026**: May payrolls beat consensus (unemployment steady at 4.3%, prior two months revised up by combined 93,000); markets re-priced toward a possible Fed rate HIKE. Gold fell more than 3% in the session — its steepest one-day drop in weeks — erasing the year's advance.
- **8 June**: Follow-through selling took gold to $4,289.9 (two-month low).
- **10 June**: May CPI came in at **4.2% y/y headline** (+0.5% m/m) with core at 2.9%; brief recovery then lower close.
- **11 June**: Gold traded near **$4,105**, with an intraday print of **$4,023.95** — the weakest level since November 2025 and roughly **26% below the January record**. Gold stands negative for the year. Silver trades near $67.

### Key Findings by Layer

**Official-sector (central bank) bid has NOT moved**: The WGC estimates Q1 2026 net additions of 244 tonnes (above both prior quarter and five-year average). 2025 net purchases were about 863 tonnes (roughly double the pre-2022 norm of 400–500). 2026 projections cluster at 750–850 tonnes. The buyer base broadened — central banks of Guatemala, Indonesia, and Malaysia entered; the Bank of Korea added gold exposure for the first time since 2013. 95% of central banks in the WGC survey expect global official gold holdings to rise. This bid is policy-driven and price-inelastic.

**Rate repricing was the main engine**: Robust payrolls and 4.2% inflation kept the Fed restrictive and lifted real yields, raising the cost of holding a non-yielding asset. BNP Paribas expects Fed hikes to begin in December 2026; TD Securities' Bart Melek notes the Fed has "virtually no inclination to cut." The dollar index pushed through 100, compounding pressure on dollar-priced gold.

**Energy prices**: Crude above $112/barrel fed the inflation prints and kept policy tight — cutting against gold's usual inflation-hedge reflex. On 9 June, crude reversed (WTI down ~4% to $87.6, Brent at $90.9), removing the supply-risk premium that had supported bullion — cutting against gold from both directions.

**Investment flows (data through 31 May)**: Global physically backed gold ETFs shed a net US$2bn in May (Europe only region with inflows at +US$334mn; Asia −US$1.2bn, North America −US$1.1bn). China drove Asia's first monthly outflow since Aug 2025; India saw US$610mn of redemptions after higher import tariffs. Total ETF assets fell 2% to US$604bn (mostly price effect) while holdings eased just 0.4% to 4,121 tonnes — barely below the 27 February record of 4,176 tonnes. YTD net flows remain positive at nearly US$17bn — financial holders sidelined but not liquidating. COMEX managed-money positioning was neutral, indicating the slide was not a forced unwind of stretched longs.

### Where Analysts Agree and Split
John notes the layoffs primarily targeted synthetic positions in the front of the curve while physical/allocated positions remained in place. Goldman Sachs attributes the selling to liquidity needs (gold as a natural source of cash during equity sell-offs), which would stop when the liquidity need stops. DataTrek Research (Nicholas Colas and Jessica Rabe) says gold simply "rallied too far, too fast." The WGC's attribution model found no standout driver in May, with a residual possibly in OTC flows.

### Transaction-Level Implications
The article emphasizes the gap between published reference prices and dealable quotes, especially in volatile conditions: spreads widen, format premiums respond to physical supply/demand independently of spot, and settlement windows price time risk. The 16–17 June Fed policy meeting is the next key test point; quoted figures have a short shelf life into it. Execution records (fixing price, date, format at execution) are essential for reconciliation during fast repricings.

# Global gold demand up 6% in third quarter 2011

---

[Back to News](/news-and-events)

---

[Back to News](/news-and-events)

[**Download***pdf* Global gold demand up 6% in third quarter 2011](/download/file/8897/GDT_Q3_2011_pr.pdf)

---

Gold demand in the third quarter of 2011 reached 1,053.9 tonnes, an increase of 6% compared to the same period last year. This equates to US$57.7bn, an all-time high in value terms.

According to the World Gold Council’s Gold Demand Trends report for Q3 2011 released today, this increase was driven by investment demand which rose by 33% year-on-year to 468.1 tonnes, generating record quarterly demand of US$25.6bn.

The report also details a number of other developments:

* Investment demand in Europe reached a record quarterly value of €4.6bn, equating to 118.1 tonnes - a year-on-year increase of 135%. The increase in overall investment demand was all the more impressive given the sharp gold price correction in September, which encouraged a wave of profit taking among bar and coin investors. Virtually all markets saw strong double-digit growth in demand for gold bars and coins.
* Chinese jewellery demand was 13% higher year-on-year at 131.0 tonnes, equivalent to RMB46.0bn. The bulk of this increase was seen in smaller cities as retail chains expanded their networks to meet increasing demand fuelled by rising income levels. China’s growing appetite for gold as a means of investment saw demand for gold bars and coins expand by 24% from year earlier levels to 60.2 tonnes.
* Jewellery demand in India was sluggish during the seasonally slow months of July and August, compounded by high inflation and greater volatility in the local gold price. Buying has since recovered slightly with the onset of the festive and wedding season. Overall, Indian jewellery demand in Q3 saw a 26% decline in tonnage, when compared to the same quarter in 2010, to 125.3 tonnes, however yearly demand to the end of September is very close to the record levels seen in 2010.

**Marcus Grubb, Managing Director, Investment at the World Gold Council commented:**

“Unsurprisingly investment demand for gold was a key driver during the third quarter. Increasing levels of inflation, the US credit rating downgrade, a worsening eurozone sovereign debt crisis and the lacklustre performance of many assets drove investors to increase holdings in gold in order to protect their wealth. Given gold’s proven risk mitigation properties, it is likely that investors will continue to seek protection from economic uncertainty, which shows no signs of abating.

“The long-term fundamentals for gold remain strong with a diverse and growing demand base coupled with constrained supply-side activity.”

### **Gold Demand Statistics for Q3 2011:**

* Global gold demand in the third quarter of 2011 increased 6% year-on-year to reach 1,053.9 tonnes, up from 991.1 tonnes in the third quarter of 2010. Gold demand in value terms was worth a record US$57.7bn up from the previous high of US$45.7bn in the preceding quarter.
* The quarterly average price rose 39% from year earlier levels to US$1,702.12, while the gold price reached a new record of US$1,895.00 (London PM Fix) on 5th and 6th September.
* Global gold investment demand reached 468.1 tonnes in the third quarter of 2011, up 33% from 352.1 tonnes in the corresponding quarter in 2010. The rise in prices led to a record US$25.6bn in value terms, almost double the US$13.9bn witnessed in Q3 2010.
* Demand for gold bars and coins increased 29% to reach 390.5 tonnes, up from 303.0 tonnes in Q3 2010. In value terms demand for bars and coins in Q3 2011 equated to US$21.4bn compared to US$12.0bn in Q3 2010.
* Gold ETFs and similar products witnessed inflows of 77.6 tonnes in the third quarter of 2011, which was 58% above year-earlier levels of 49.1 tonnes.
* Global demand for gold jewellery of 465.6 tonnes in the third quarter of 2011 was 10% below year-earlier levels of 518.9 tonnes. In value terms demand reached a quarterly record of US$25.5bn, 24% higher than the third quarter of 2010, which registered US$20.5bn.
* In spite of challenging market conditions, gold demand from the global technology sector showed significant resilience and was flat year-on-year at 120.2 tonnes. In value terms demand from the electronics sector was equivalent to a record US$4.8bn.
* Central bank net purchases amounted to 148.4 tonnes, as they continued to increase their allocation to gold as a percentage of total reserves.
* Gold supply was 1,034.4 tonnes in the third quarter of 2011, 2% higher than year-earlier levels of 1,013.0 tonnes. Mine production increased by 5% to 746.2 tonnes from 710.9 tonnes during the third quarter of 2010.
* Despite record prices being reached during the quarter, recycling activity was relatively modest. Third quarter 2011 gold recycling accounted for 426.5 tonnes of supply, up 13% year-on-year from 379.1 tonnes.

A copy of the Q3 2011 Gold Demand Trends report, which includes comprehensive data, can be viewed at: [www.gold.org/supply-and-demand/gold-demand-trends](/supply-and-demand/gold-demand-trends).
