URL: https://www.chicagofed.org/publications/chicago-fed-letter/2021/464

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Chicago Fed Letter (No. 464, November 2021) by Robert Barsky, Craig Epstein, Adrian Lafont-Mueller, and Younggeun Yoo examines what drives gold prices since the U.S. dollar price of gold was allowed to float freely in 1971. The article identifies three key drivers commonly cited: inflationary expectations, real interest rates, and pessimism about future macroeconomic conditions. The authors organize their empirical evidence around three claims: gold is a hedge against inflation, gold is sensitive to expected long-term real interest rates, and gold is seen as protective against "bad economic times."

Using multiple regression analyses across three specifications — annual levels (1971–2019), quarterly innovations (VAR), and daily differences (2003–2021) — the authors find:
- In the annual levels regression, a 1 percentage point rise in long-term real interest rates lowers real gold prices by 13.1%, while an extra percentage point of ten-year expected inflation raises real gold prices by 37%. Real world GDP has a coefficient of 1.125, and a one standard deviation increase (8.1 points) in pessimistic survey responses raises gold prices by 9.7%.
- In the quarterly innovations regression, a 1 percentage point innovation in expected ten-year real interest rates is associated with a 3.4% reduction in real gold prices, while innovations in PTR (inflation expectations) play no significant role. A 10 percentage point innovation in pessimistic expectations raises real gold prices by 5%.
- In the daily regression using TIPS yields, a 1 percentage point change in TIPS yield lowers gold prices by 1.1%, while a 1 percentage point change in break-even inflation raises prices by 2.7%.

Key findings: The negative effect of real interest rates on gold prices predicted by theory holds in all three contexts. Two of three specifications support the inflation hedge view, with the inflation effect quantitatively larger than the real interest rate effect. In the early part of the sample (1971–2000), variation in inflation or inflationary expectations was the single most important driver; from 2001 onward, long-term real interest rates and pessimism about future economic activity became dominant. During 2001–2012, the long-term real interest rate fell about 400 basis points while real gold prices rose more than fivefold. The authors conclude that disinflation since 2001 might have been expected to produce low gold prices, but any such effect was more than offset by unprecedentedly low long-term real interest rates and pessimism about economic activity.

URL: https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/files/monetary20260729a1.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On July 29, 2026, the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) voted 9-3 to maintain the federal funds rate target range at 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent, in support of the Federal Reserve's dual mandate. The Committee continues its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system. The statement notes that economic activity is expanding at a solid pace despite elevated uncertainty partly due to the Middle East conflict, with strong productivity growth and capital investment. Job gains have kept pace with the workforce and the unemployment rate has changed little, though inflation remains elevated relative to the 2 percent goal, partly reflecting supply shocks that have driven up prices in certain sectors including energy. The Committee affirmed it will deliver price stability.

Voting against the action were Beth M. Hammack, Neel Kashkari, and Lorie K. Logan, who preferred to raise the target range by 1/4 percentage point at this meeting.

In implementing the monetary policy stance (effective July 30, 2026):
• The Board of Governors voted unanimously to maintain the interest rate paid on reserve balances at 3.65 percent.
• The FOMC directed the Open Market Desk to maintain the federal funds rate in the 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent range; conduct standing overnight repurchase agreement operations at 3.75 percent; conduct standing overnight reverse repurchase agreement operations at 3.5 percent with a per-counterparty limit of $160 billion per day; purchase Treasury bills and other short-term Treasury securities as needed to maintain ample reserves; roll over principal payments from Treasury securities holdings; and reinvest principal payments from agency securities into Treasury bills.
• The Board of Governors voted unanimously to establish the primary credit rate at the existing level of 3.75 percent.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a MUFG (Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group) research note published August 20, 2026, by analysts George Goncalves and Agron Nicaj, updating their Federal Reserve and US rates forecast. The core thesis is that the Fed will remain on hold for the balance of 2026 (no hikes and no cuts), pushing easing expectations into early 2027.

Key points:
1. The authors do not see urgency to restart rate hikes and expect the Fed to remain on hold through 2026.
2. They have pushed back their easing expectations into early 2027.
3. Each tenor point estimate was revised higher by 25-50bps across the forecast horizon.
4. They argue the US rates market is in an "overshoot mode" that is creating value in the bond market.

Macro rationale: Data has looked notably weaker since the last FOMC meeting, with both nonfarm payrolls (NFP) and retail sales growth negative in July. While core CPI rebounded in July after a weak June (inflation hasn't eased enough to fully dissuade hawks), wage growth has fallen to levels consistent with 2% inflation, with little added thrust from tariffs and energy prices going forward.

Markets perspective: Rate hike expectations have declined while long-term rates have meaningfully increased, "doing some of the tightening for the Fed." The authors do not see inflationary pressures re-surfacing strongly enough to warrant immediate hikes, noting this is largely a supply shock environment.

Fed rate path implications: Hawkish tension at the Fed will keep near-term rate hike expectations priced-in but not delivered. Rate hike expectations won't fully fade until resolution of the US/Iran war or a material drop in inflation; they will trade in a 30-60% probability range of a 25bp hike at each upcoming FOMC meeting. As 2027 approaches, markets are expected to pivot back to pricing in cuts.

Forecast table (Q3-2026 through Q2-2027):
- Fed Funds Rate: 3.625 → 3.625 → 3.375 → 3.125
- US 2-Year: 4.125 → 3.875 → 3.625 → 3.500
- US 5-Year: 4.250 → 4.125 → 3.875 → 3.750
- US 10-Year: 4.500 → 4.375 → 4.250 → 4.125
- US 30-Year: 5.000 → 4.875 → 4.625 → 4.500

The authors maintain a checklist heading into the Jackson Hole Symposium and September FOMC meeting to steer their Fed view. The website includes disclaimers that materials are produced only for professional investors, are not investment research or investment advice.

--- SOURCE 4: Fed meeting recap: July 2026 ---
URL: https://www.cnbc.com/2026/07/29/fed-meeting-today-live-updates.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a CNBC live blog covering the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) decision and Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh's news conference on Wednesday, July 29, 2026.

**Key Decision:** The Fed kept its benchmark interest rate unchanged at 3.5% to 3.75%. Three policymakers dissented in favor of a rate hike—Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan, Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, and Minneapolis Fed President Neel Kashkari—marking the first time since September 2016 that three voters dissented. Governor Christopher Waller also made statements supportive of tighter policy.

**Warsh's Comments:** Warsh said the Fed "will not hesitate to act" to meet its 2% inflation goal but declined to provide forward guidance or hints on rate policy. He insisted the decision was not a "pause" but "a rigorous review of the economic situation." He acknowledged a "good family fight" over the decision and reiterated: "We will deliver price stability." Warsh noted the Fed "doesn't always need to be the center of attention" and welcomed markets reacting to real data. He confirmed press conferences will continue for 2026 and said his Jackson Hole keynote speech (Aug. 27-29) is currently "a blank piece of paper" but may be informed by the five policy task forces he created.

**Market Reaction:** Stocks fell after the decision (S&P 500 down 0.6%, Nasdaq down 0.5%, Dow down ~840 points/1.6%). The 30-year Treasury yield topped 5.2%, the highest since 2007, while the 10-year yield rose above 7 basis points to 4.677%. Bond yields jumped following the meeting despite the hold.

**Inflation Context:** June CPI posted a surprise 0.4% drop, but the Middle East conflict (U.S. vs. Iran) has reversed the decline in gas prices. Brent crude jumped more than 15% month-to-date in July and more than 38% in 2026 due to Strait of Hormuz disruptions. The average gallon of unleaded gas hit $4.09, up 6% from a month ago.

**Expert Reactions:**
- President Trump claimed Warsh "would love to see lower interest rates" but is held back by a "political board."
- Indeed economist Aubrey Woessner said the labor market is "playing second fiddle" to inflation.
- Vanguard's Adam Schickling expects rate hikes to be "difficult this year" due to a cooling labor market.
- Goldman Sachs' Kay Haigh said a September hike is "finely balanced," dependent on Middle East developments and the next two CPI prints.
- Thornburg's Christian Hoffmann called it an "uncomfortable hold."
- FWDBONDS' Chris Rupkey criticized the Fed for showing "no sign of taking steps" to control inflation.
- Citadel Securities expected a surprise hike; Fundstrat's Tom Lee expected a hold.
- Former Fed Governor Stephen Miran said rates should stay on hold, viewing current inflation as "transitory" and driven by temporary war effects.

**Other Notes:** Wall Street is adjusting to the "Warsh era" of less communication—F/m Investments launched "WarshGPT," an AI bot to interpret Warsh. Fed CEO Hassett said Warsh's stewardship is "already a home run." Federal Reserve Governor Stephen Miran (served Sept 2025–May 2026) argued for holding rates.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"I understand the desire for rolling forecasts and commentary from this committee, but for our part, we need to observe market reaction to developments direct and unfiltered. I want to stress, of course, that decisions by this committee matter a great deal, and where necessary and appropriate, we will not hesitate to act." — Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The Federal Reserve System (the Fed) is the central banking system of the United States, established on December 23, 1913, through the Federal Reserve Act following a series of financial panics (especially the severe 1907 crisis) that created a desire for central control of the American monetary system. Although an instrument of the U.S. government, the Fed is considered an independent central bank due to its structural insulation from political interference. Events such as the Great Depression and the Great Recession have expanded its remit over the years.

Congress established three key objectives for monetary policy: maximizing employment, stabilizing prices (interpreted as an average inflation rate of 2 percent per year), and moderating long-term interest rates (the first two comprise the "dual mandate"). Its duties also include supervising and regulating banks, maintaining financial system stability, and providing financial services to depository institutions, the U.S. government, and foreign official institutions. The Fed also conducts economic research and publishes the Beige Book and the FRED database.

The system is multi-layered: governed by the presidentially appointed Board of Governors (FRB) in Washington, D.C., with twelve regional Federal Reserve Banks regulating and overseeing privately owned commercial banks. The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) sets monetary policy by adjusting the target federal funds rate. Key current leadership includes Chair Kevin Warsh, Vice Chair Philip Jefferson, and Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman. Current rates: bank rate 3.75%, interest rate target 3.50–3.75%, interest on reserves 3.65%; reserve requirements are now none.

Purposes include addressing banking panics, serving as central bank, balancing private interests of banks with centralized government responsibility, supervising banking institutions, protecting consumer credit rights, conducting monetary policy, maintaining financial system stability, and providing financial services. The Fed operates under a fractional-reserve banking system and serves as lender of last resort. It was designed as a compromise between privatized and government-regulated banking philosophies—agrarian/progressive interests (led by William Jennings Bryan) favored public control while the nation's bankers opposed political appointees, resulting in a hybrid public-private, centralized-decentralized structure.

As the government's bank, the Fed processes trillions in financial transactions, handles Treasury checking accounts and federal tax deposits, issues currency (the Bureau of Engraving and Printing delivered 57.95 billion notes in FY2020 at 7.4 cents per note), and sells/redeems U.S. government securities. The Board supervises approximately 900 state member banks and 5,000 bank holding companies, oversees consumer protection laws (Truth in Lending, Equal Credit Opportunity, Home Mortgage Disclosure Acts), and can be audited by the Government Accountability Office (GAO) through the 1978 Federal Banking Agency Audit Act. The Fed's monetary policy tools include the federal funds rate, interest on reserve balances, open market operations, discount window, term deposit facility, and quantitative easing. Historical crisis tools include reserve requirements (since expired) and crisis facilities from 2008 (term auction facility, commercial paper funding facility, etc.). The Fed has faced criticism over inflation management, transparency, and its role in economic downturns, with some calling for its abolition.
</summary>

However, the vast majority of the nation's bankers, concerned about government intervention in the banking business, opposed a central bank structure directed by political appointees. The legislation that Congress ultimately adopted in 1913 reflected a hard-fought battle to balance these two competing views and created the hybrid public-private, centralized-decentralized structure that we have today." - Donald L. Kohn (2006), vice chairman of the Board of Governors
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Bullion Exchanges (published February 23, 2026) examines why gold and silver lease rates - the annualized cost to borrow physical bullion in wholesale markets like LBMA and COMEX - are elevated in 2026, signaling tighter deliverable supply rather than depletion of global inventories.

Key data points:
- Gold spot price trading above $5,000/oz; silver near mid-$80s/oz
- Gold lease rates: 1.0%-2.0% annualized depending on tenor
- Silver lease rates: 6%-7%+ in short tenors, with brief February spikes

Gold lease rate drivers: central bank accumulation reducing floating inventory, ETF/institutional inflows removing metal from lending, macro risk hedging, and collateral preference (institutions holding gold outright rather than leasing for minimal yield).

Silver lease rate drivers (more volatile than gold): industrial demand surge (solar panels, EV components, electronics), persistent structural supply deficits, inventory migration between London and COMEX vault systems creating localized scarcity, backwardation signals (immediate delivery prices above futures), and speculative/ETF flows. Silver's smaller, thinner wholesale market makes it inherently more sensitive to demand surges.

Supply chain components: form mismatch (institutional bars vs. retail products), geographic mismatch (metal in London vs. demand in New York/Asia), refining bottlenecks from scrap flow surges, and transportation/settlement delays - all contributing to elevated lease rates.

Historical perspective: lease rate spikes occurred during the 1980 Hunt Brothers silver crisis, 2008 financial crisis, 2020 pandemic (London-New York dislocations), and 2025 trade/tariff volatility (silver spikes exceeding 20%-30% annualized). Compared to these episodes, 2026 rates are orderly and far below systemic crisis levels.

Investor takeaways: elevated lease rates indicate strong physical demand and localized tightness, not scarcity. Gold leasing remains stable/controlled; silver leasing is tighter due to industrial factors. Markets historically rebalance over time. The article includes FAQs covering lease rate definitions, why silver rates exceed gold, backwardation, and investor implications.

URL: https://www.nycbullion.com/blog/post/silver-shortage-signals-comex-vs-lbma-inventory-clues.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This NYC Bullion blog article examines silver shortage signals by analyzing inventory data from COMEX (futures market) and LBMA (London wholesale vaults). 

Key points:
- Silver differs from gold as it trades as both a monetary metal and industrial material (used in solar panels, electronics, EVs, medical devices, defense, and emerging tech).
- COMEX inventory is split into "registered" (metal with warrants attached, deliverable against futures) and "eligible" (meets exchange standards but no active warrant, not automatically deliverable). The registered/eligible ratio is central to assessing delivery readiness.
- LBMA provides monthly data on total London vault holdings but does not divide into registered/eligible categories and does not show immediately available metal.
- COMEX and LBMA answer different questions—COMEX for delivery mechanics, LBMA for wholesale inventory trends—and should not be treated as competing truth sources.
- No single indicator proves a shortage. A serious warning sign requires confirmation from multiple signals: falling COMEX registered stocks, declining LBMA holdings, rising delivery demand, stronger physical premiums, ETF outflows, elevated lease rates, and persistent global deficits.
- Silver supply is constrained: mine supply responds slowly to prices (much is mined as a byproduct of copper, lead, zinc, and gold), and global supply has struggled to keep pace with demand.
- Demand drivers include solar energy, electronics, automotive, AI infrastructure, 5G, medical equipment, defense, plus investment demand from coins, bars, rounds, and ETFs.
- Retail availability is separate from wholesale vault data—coins and bars require fabrication, so premiums and delivery delays can rise even when wholesale bars remain plentiful.
- Bullion buyers should watch product premiums, delivery times, mint supply, dealer inventories, and buyback spreads alongside vault data.
- Silver shortages can be localized; the market is connected but not perfectly uniform.

The article includes a detailed FAQ section covering what shortage signals are, definitions of COMEX registered/eligible silver, the registered-to-eligible ratio, LBMA vs COMEX differences, whether falling registered silver proves a shortage, why retail silver can seem scarce despite high vault inventories, the role of industrial demand, and which indicator is most important.

The article was published June 10, 2026, and includes related blog links on inflation's effect on precious metals, .999 vs .9999 gold purity, platinum's relationship with gold, and online bullion dealer comparisons.
</summary>

<summary>
This World Gold Council (WGC) analysis (February 2025) examines whether US tariff threats are moving the gold market. Key highlights: COMEX gold inventories have surged nearly 300t (registered) and over 500t (eligible) since late 2024, driven by traders pre-emptively shipping gold to the US to avoid potential broad-based tariffs — despite gold not being directly targeted. This coincided with the spread between COMEX futures and spot gold reaching US$40-50/oz (140-180 bps), significantly above the two-year average of US$13/oz (60 bps), mirroring patterns seen during COVID. London LBMA inventories fell but remain at ~8,500t (5,200t at Bank of England), with bank queues reflecting logistics constraints rather than scarcity. Gold lease rates spiked to nearly 5% in January before cooling to ~1%. The WGC argues this is largely a risk-management phenomenon rather than a true supply issue, citing gold's diverse global supply sources (Switzerland, Canada, Latin America, Australia) and signs of normalization—COMEX inventory buildup slowing, spread differentials falling, ETF bid-ask spreads well-behaved. Gold's price strength has been supported by flight-to-quality flows amid geopolitical/geoeconomic volatility, with gold ETFs seeing US$10.3bn inflows (113t) in 2025's strongest two-month period in two years. The WGC expects disruptions to ease over coming weeks but warns that temporary distortions may recur amid elevated geoeconomic risk, while noting the gold market's depth and liquidity can absorb most shocks.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We believe that the disruptions will likely ease…although the current environment of elevated geoeconomic risks could result in intermittent spikes" "Even indirect trade policy concerns can send ripples through global financial markets. This may not be the last time we see temporary distortions in the gold market." "It's an obvious point, but gold is a physical asset, so there are real logistical constraints and security constraints." — Dave Ramsden, Deputy Governor for Markets and Banking at the Bank of England "The sign of the depth and liquidity of the gold market is able to absorb – over time – most of these shocks." The movement of gold from London to the US, rising COMEX premiums and concerns over availability were largely the result of risk management decisions rather than true supply issues.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: Fed Cuts Rates and Signals More to Come in 2025 | Morningstar ---
URL: https://www.morningstar.com/economy/fed-cuts-rates-signals-more-come-2025

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The Federal Reserve cut the federal-funds rate by 0.25 percentage points to a target range of 4.00%-4.25%, a move widely expected since the August jobs report showed sharp deterioration in job growth. The central bank's press release noted the committee "judges that downside risks to employment have risen."

The cut was not unanimous—11 of 12 FOMC members voted for a quarter-point cut, with Stephen Miran being the lone voter for a half-point cut. Miran, recently confirmed to the Board of Governors after serving as chair of the Council of Economic Advisers in the Trump administration, likely accounts for the dot plot projection of a 2.75%-3.00% rate by end of 2025 (another 1.25 points in cuts). His advocacy for looser policy aligns with President Trump's desires, though he doesn't endorse Trump's stated goal of a 1.25%-1.50% range. Miran's term runs through January 2026, and a reappointment could give him a fresh 14-year term. Fed Chair Jerome Powell affirmed that independence is "deeply in [the Federal Reserve's] culture."

The broader FOMC projections show a median expectation of 3.50%-3.75% by end of 2025 (in line with market expectations) and 3.25%-3.50% by end of 2026 (only one 0.25-point cut in 2026, while the market expected 0.75 points). Morningstar is in between, expecting 3.00%-3.25% at end of 2026.

On economic projections, the FOMC expects core inflation at 2.6% year-over-year by end of 2026, while Morningstar expects 3.2% due to tariffs. The FOMC projects unemployment at 4.4% in Q4 2026 vs. Morningstar's 4.7%, and GDP growth at 1.6% vs. Morningstar's 1.3%. Given that inflationary effects from tariffs are expected to be a one-off shock counterbalanced by increasing economic slack, labor market risks call for looser monetary policy.

Powell described a labor market in a state of precarious balance, noting unemployment has averaged 4.2% over the past three months vs. 4.1% in Q1 2025. Both labor supply and demand have fallen; if demand keeps contracting, the economy risks a vicious cycle of layoffs and spending contraction.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
The central bank's official press release noted that the committee "judges that downside risks to employment have risen," and said they decided to cut "in light of the shift in the balance of risks.", The broader set of FOMC projections shows that the median participant expects the rate to hit 3.50%-3.75% by the end of 2025, in line with current market expectations., Fed Chair Jerome Powell affirmed that independence is "deeply in [the Federal Reserve's] culture" and can't be overturned overnight., Both labor supply and demand have fallen, keeping unemployment from changing much. But if demand continues contracting, the economy risks toppling into a vicious cycle of layoffs and contraction of spending.

# Jackson Hole Is 14 Days Away. What Warsh Says Could Move Gold More Than Any Inflation Print.

Published: 08-13-2026, 03:38 pm

Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh told reporters after the July 29 meeting that he wanted his Jackson Hole speech to “frame the big questions.” He noted that the constant cycle of meetings and press conferences creates a tendency to “get caught up in the myopic” — his word — debating quarter-point moves rather than the structural forces shaping the next decade. He also said the Fed is “not constrained by market prices.” For gold investors, those two statements contain everything worth watching between now and August 27.

Gold is trading near $4,356 today, down about 1.2% from yesterday’s two-month high of $4,450. That pullback follows a week when [two consecutive months of cooling inflation](https://goldsilver.com/industry-news/goldsilver-news/gold-price-ppi-cpi-fed-september/) drove September rate-hike odds sharply lower. July PPI came in flat month-over-month, well below the 0.2% consensus. July CPI rose just 0.1% month-over-month. Together, those prints pushed CME FedWatch’s implied probability of a September hike from roughly 54% a week ago to approximately 39% today.

## Why Jackson Hole Matters More Than the Inflation Data

The drop in rate-hike odds drove gold’s recovery this week. Lower hike expectations compress real yields — the inflation-adjusted return on Treasuries — which reduces the opportunity cost of holding gold and pushes the price higher. That mechanism is why gold broke above its 100-day moving average at $4,387 for the first time in more than two months. But the same mechanism runs in reverse, and Jackson Hole is the next event that could flip it.

The symposium runs August 27–29. Warsh will speak as Fed Chair for the first time since taking office on May 22, 2026. Under Warsh, the Fed no longer telegraphs its intentions ahead of meetings, so a major speech from this chair carries genuine information value. He told reporters on July 29 that his remarks will focus on long-term structural questions, not near-term guidance — but he also made clear the Fed will act independently of what markets are pricing. That 39% September hike probability does not bind him.

![Gold & Silver News Nuggets](https://goldsilver.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/The-Nuggets-Newsletter.png)

## The Edge Every Investor Needs Smarter precious metals investing starts here. The Nuggets Newsletter brings you essential market insights, Fed updates, global trends, educational videos, and much more.

### A Split Committee and a Missing Dot

The July 29 FOMC vote was 9–3 to hold at 3.50%–3.75%. Three voting members — Beth Hammack, Neel Kashkari, and Lorie Logan — dissented in favor of an immediate hike. That level of dissent at only Warsh’s second meeting as chair signals a vocal minority believes the hold is already a mistake. In June, nine of eighteen participants who submitted economic projections penciled in at least one hike before year-end. Warsh withheld his own dot. Markets consequently have no read on where the chair’s baseline sits, which is precisely what makes his August 27 speech the most important data point of the month.

#### The Second Corner: Why This Is Bigger Than One Rate Decision

Today’s pullback is not a reversal. Gold holds above its 100-day moving average, and the rate data is moving in gold’s direction. However, the deeper story here is not about September at all.

US public debt stands at approximately $39.89 trillion, according to Treasury Fiscal Data. The Congressional Budget Office projects net interest payments will reach roughly $1.0 trillion in FY2026 — matching the base defense appropriation for the first time. Every 25 basis point rate increase adds tens of billions more to that annual cost. That constraint does not appear in any inflation print, and it means the Fed is managing not just prices but the refinancing risk of a sovereign balance sheet with no easy exit. Central banks understand this. They purchased 288.9 tonnes of gold in Q2 2026 — up 62% year-over-year and the strongest second quarter on record, per the World Gold Council — buying into a quarter when gold prices were falling.

Physical gold has no credit risk and pays no interest. It sits entirely outside the fiscal trap the Fed is navigating. Before Jackson Hole, also watch the University of Michigan inflation expectations survey on August 14 and the July PCE release in late August — both will shape the hawks’ case heading into Warsh’s speech. Watch $4,450 as near-term resistance. A close above it, particularly if Warsh leans toward the long-run framework, would suggest markets are settling on a September hold as the base case.

This is a GoldSilver.com news article (published August 13, 2026) analyzing why Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh's upcoming Jackson Hole speech on August 27, 2026 is poised to be a bigger catalyst for gold prices than any single inflation print.

**Key events and data:**
- Gold was trading near $4,356, down ~1.2% from a two-month high of $4,450 set the prior day.
- Two consecutive months of cooling inflation drove September Fed rate-hike odds sharply lower: July PPI was flat month-over-month (well below 0.2% consensus), and July CPI rose just 0.1% month-over-month.
- CME FedWatch implied probability of a September rate hike fell from ~54% a week earlier to ~39% on August 13 (it had been 46% after the July 29 FOMC meeting).
- Lower rate-hike expectations compress real yields, reducing the opportunity cost of holding gold and pushing prices higher—the mechanism that drove gold above its 100-day moving average at $4,387 for the first time in over two months.

**The Jackson Hole significance:**
- The symposium runs August 27–29, 2026. Warsh will speak as Fed Chair for the first time since taking office on May 22, 2026.
- Under Warsh, the Fed no longer telegraphs intentions ahead of meetings, giving the speech genuine information value. He stated he wants the speech to "frame the big questions" and that the Fed is "not constrained by market prices."
- The July 29 FOMC vote was 9–3 to hold rates at 3.50%–3.75%. Dissenters (Beth Hammack, Neel Kashkari, Lorie Logan) favored an immediate hike. In June, nine of eighteen participants penciled in at least one hike before year-end, and Warsh withheld his own dot—leaving markets without a read on his baseline.

**Structural/fiscal context:**
- US public debt stands at ~$39.89 trillion; CBO projects net interest payments of ~$1.0 trillion in FY2026, matching the base defense appropriation for the first time. Every 25 bps rate increase adds tens of billions to that annual cost.
- Central banks purchased 288.9 tonnes of gold in Q2 2026, up 62% year-over-year and the strongest second quarter on record (World Gold Council), buying even as gold prices were falling.
- Physical gold carries no credit risk and pays no interest, sitting outside the fiscal trap the Fed is navigating.

**Levels/events to watch:**
- University of Michigan inflation expectations survey on August 14 and July PCE release in late August will shape the hawks' case.
- $4,450 is near-term resistance; a close above it, especially if Warsh leans toward the long-run framework, suggests markets are settling on a September hold as the base case.

**Sources cited:** BLS (PPI/CPI), Federal Reserve FOMC materials, Kansas City Fed (Jackson Hole), CME FedWatch, World Gold Council, US Treasury Fiscal Data, CBO, KPMG, and GoldSilver spot prices.

The article also promotes GoldSilver's "Nuggets Newsletter" and includes related articles on gold prices, PPI/CPI impacts, China's gold buying, and silver targets (Citi put a $90 target on silver).

From a long-term perspective, gold has tested the 0.272 Fibonacci retracement of the 1920–2026 secular uptrend.

This level represents a potentially historic inflection point on the chart, serving either as a major long-term dip-buying opportunity or as confirmation of a deeper corrective phase.

**Rebound or Deeper Corrective Cycle?**

A sustained rebound from this area would reinforce the broader secular uptrend that has defined gold's performance over the last several years.

Conversely, a confirmed breakdown could expose the next major support zone near 3500, which previously acted as a significant resistance area throughout much of 2025.

The key question remains whether gold can reclaim bullish momentum above 4360 while the US Dollar Index holds near critical resistance levels.

With DXY still respecting long-term trend support and markets reassessing the outlook for rate cuts under Kevin Warsh, the battle between dollar strength and gold resilience remains one of the most important themes to watch during the second half of 2026.

- Bullish scenario: A sustained daily/weekly close above 4370 with daily momentum back above the neutral 50 level confirms medium-term bullish continuation. Upside targets: 4470 (78.6%) and 4590 (100%). A breakout beyond 4590 confirms the longer-term bullish case.
- Bearish scenario: A close below 4280 could fill the week's opening gap and expose support at 4220 and 4150. Further breakdown brings yearly lows near 4080 and 4020 into focus, with a deeper corrective move toward 3880 (October 2025 low).
- Long-term: Gold has tested the 0.272 Fibonacci retracement of the 1920–2026 secular uptrend—a potentially historic inflection point serving either as a major long-term dip-buying opportunity or confirmation of a deeper correction.
- A confirmed breakdown could expose the next major support near 3500 (previously significant resistance throughout much of 2025).

The core question remains whether gold can reclaim bullish momentum above 4360 while the DXY holds near critical resistance levels, with the battle between dollar strength and gold resilience being a key theme for the second half of 2026.

# Where gold price is headed next as Fed rate hike and inflation odds change direction

[Kevin Williams](https://www.cnbc.com/kevin-williams/)

[WATCH LIVE](/live-tv/)

Key Points

* The price of gold has experienced big swings in 2026 after hitting a record early in the year above $5,000.
* Last week, the precious metal, along with silver, turned in its best performance in months.
* Tamer inflation data and declining odds of a Fed rate hike contributed to the rally, but short-term volatility in the gold trade may persist.

In this article

* [@GC.1](/quotes/@GC.1)
* [GDX](/quotes/GDX)
* [GDXJ](/quotes/GDXJ)
* [@SI.1](/quotes/@SI.1)
* [IAU](/quotes/IAU)
* [SLV](/quotes/SLV)
* [GLD](/quotes/GLD)

Courtesy: Kinross

In 2026, [gold](/quotes/@GC.1/) has been a tough trade to time right, falling from a 10-year high over $5,300 an ounce that it reached early in the year by as much as 18%, according to [Goldprice.org](https://goldprice.org/). But last week was the precious metal's best week since January, while gold mining stocks had their hottest five-day run since 2008. With volatility in the gold trade leaving it with a year-to-date return that is now close to flat, some are betting that the trading chart direction is going to continue up. But there are potential pitfalls ahead. After all, even with its recent [dramatic moves](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/07/gold-bugs-spend-180-million-betting-alls-clear-for-metal-as-bond-yields-stall.html), the price of gold is still higher by over $1,000 in the past one-year period.

"Gold is the new gold," said Pippa Malmgren, a former Special Assistant to President George W. Bush and member of the National Economic Council.

Malmgren says what has attracted investors to gold has not changed. Many are scared that fiscal spending is [out of control in the U.S.](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/04/28/jamie-dimon-bond-crisis-global-debt-risks.html) and that growth will be weak everywhere else. "This implies inflation," Malmgren said. She added that the Trump administration's pursuit of [expensive foreign wars](https://www.ms.now/news/iran-war-cost-trump), as well as its embrace of cryptocurrencies, both add to uneasiness among some investors.

"This makes nervous investors turn to conservative methods for preserving value, such as buying gold," Malmgren said. Central banks around the world, meanwhile, are expanding their gold holdings, which she says further signals a loss of confidence in fiat money, led by [continued buying of gold](https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/chinas-gold-reserves-rise-by-most-since-october-2023-buying-pace-quickens-2026-08-07/) by China.

"Central banks never stopped buying," said Patrick Kennedy, founder and managing partner of Hartford, Connecticut-based AllSource Investment Managementd. "The PBOC added 19.9 tons in July, its largest month since October 2023 and its 21st straight month of accumulation," Kennedy said.

That bullishness is shared by billionaire hedge fund manager [John Paulson](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/07/22/john-paulson-says-we-are-in-early-stages-of-a-long-term-bull-market-for-gold.html), who recently told CNBC that gold is only in early stages of a long-term rally, citing loss of faith in paper currency and runaway government spending (Paulson has been a gold bull since 2009).

![John Paulson: Gold in the early stages of a long-term bull market](https://image.cnbcfm.com/api/v1/image/108338676-17847416871784741684-47324076402-1080pnbcnews.jpg?v=1784741686&w=750&h=422&vtcrop=y)

watch now

VIDEO2:5602:56

John Paulson: Gold in the early stages of a long-term bull market

[The Exchange](https://www.cnbc.com/the-exchange/)

While fear has been a driver of the gold rush mentality historically, Joe Cavatoni, senior market strategist at the World Gold Council, says he views the recent bounce among U.S. investors as more of an opportunistic trade.

"Gold's recent rebound appears to be driven more by changing expectations around interest rates and the economy than by fear alone," Cavatoni said. "There are signs of weakening, particularly on the jobs front, and markets are responding quickly. As investors adjust their outlook for rates, gold is reacting the way you'd expect a highly macro-sensitive asset to respond," Cavatoni said.

"My sense is that the U.S. flows driving this move are more tactical in nature, as we have seen [GLD options activity increase](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/10/gold-just-had-its-best-week-in-7-months-heres-why-mike-khouw-is-buying-more.html), while the buying we're seeing out of Asia and Europe tends to be stickier," Cavatoni said, referring to flows into the SPDR Gold Shares ETF ([GLD](/quotes/GLD/)), with investors in both regions adding to their holdings.

With expectations for a rate hike from the Federal Reserve coming down after [the latest inflation data](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/12/cpi-inflation-report-july-2026.html) was viewed by the market as tame, the appeal of gold versus other rate-sensitive assets and against a soft U.S. dollar typically increases.

"I wouldn't view gold simply as a safe-haven asset. Many investors are using it as a wealth preservation tool and to help diversify portfolios amid ongoing uncertainty about growth and policy," Cavatoni said.

Kennedy says that the recent flows into ETFs, which reached a six-week high, is professional money, not just retail chasing.

GLD was higher by roughly 1% on Wednesday.

![hide content](https://static-redesign.cnbcfm.com/dist/a54b41835a8b60db28c2.svg)

Performance of the SPDR Gold Shares ETF over the past five-year period.

[Expectations for a rate hike](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/07/odds-the-fed-hikes-in-september-tumble-following-big-july-jobs-miss.html) were declining even before the latest inflation print, said Nick Cawley, a contributing analyst for Solomon Global, a UK-based gold and silver bullion dealer, down by over 20-percentage points in the past week.

"This suggests markets are growing more cautious about further U.S. rate increases," he said, pointing to the recent benign trend in the inflation data and last Friday's soft non-farm payrolls report.

Kennedy says his firm's view was that the first half selloff in gold was a buying opportunity rather than the sign of a top. "We bought and added to GLDM off the July technical bottom," he said, referring to another share class of GLD which has a lower expense ratio.

But he says declining expectations for a rate hike are not the same as a Fed positioned to cut. "This is not a rate cut trade, at least not yet. The Fed has been parked at 3.50 to 3.75 all year and September was genuinely live for a hike right up until the payrolls miss," Kennedy said.

"What changed is that the hike tail risk came out of the market," Kennedy said, noting this morning's CPI at 0.1 percent monthly and 3.4 percent annual, with core at 2.5 percent, was in line and keeps that narrative going. "It's a different setup than a cutting cycle, and it matters when you're asking whether this has legs," Kennedy added.

From a technical standpoint, last week's move above the 50-day moving average, along with the break of this year's pattern of lower highs, should support further gains, Cawley said, with any pullbacks expected to be short-lived and viewed as opportunities to re-enter gold's next leg higher.

### Gold miners see increased investor interest

Some traders and investors have turned to the trade in gold mining stocks in a search for value within the equities market, said Vince Stanzione, an independent trade and author of "The Millionaire Dropout."

"Many quality mining stocks are trading on single digit forward P/Es and paying great dividends," Stanzione said, pointing to [AngloGold Ashanti](/quotes/AU/) and S&P 500 member [Newmont](/quotes/NEM/). He added that many retail traders prefer to use ETFs, with the most popular being Van Eck Gold Miners ([GDX](/quotes/GDX/)), which covers the larger mining stocks, and Van Eck Junior Gold Miners ([GDXJ](/quotes/GDXJ/)), which covers the junior miners.

"Many gold miners also have exposure to silver as well, which moves in sync with gold," Stanzione said. Last week, [silver](/quotes/@SI.1/) has its best week since February.

## ETF Strategist full coverage:

Here's a look at other stories offering insight on ETFs for investors.

* [Investors made easy money on oil bets during Iran war. The trade is getting trickier](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/02/oil-prices-iran-war-energy-market.html)
* [For Gen X investors nearing retirement, the dotcom bubble looms large](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/07/26/gen-x-investors-dotcom-bubble-retirement-portfolio.html)
* [Jamie Dimon made a bearish treasuries call. Investors were all over it](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/07/21/jamie-dimon-stock-bond-market-warning-treasuries.html)
* [How to prepare a tech-heavy portfolio with record gains for an inevitable downturn](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/07/21/market-bubble-stock-risks-investing-mistakes.html)
* [Trump Accounts are good start, but shouldn't be a child's only investment](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/07/31/trump-accounts-children-stock-market-investing.html)

For retail investors, there are multiple options to implement a bullish trade on gold, according to Shawn Young, chief analyst at MEXC Research, which is a cryptocurrency trade platform. Bullion ETFs such as GLD and iShares Gold Trust ([IAU](/quotes/IAU/)) are the most direct way to express the gold view, Young said.

GLDM, the preferred gold ETF of Kennedy, has an expense ratio of 10 basis points versus 40 for GLD, with IAU in between at 25 basis points. "GLDM is the cheaper vehicle if you're buying and holding while GLD is the better instrument if you want liquidity and options," he said.

The iShares Silver Trust ([SLV](/quotes/SLV/)) offers a more volatile route into precious metals, according to Young, while GDX and GDXJ offer operating leverage and equity risk beyond the underlying metal's price swings.

That leverage cuts both ways, according to Young: when gold prices climb while mining costs hold steady, profit margins can expand much faster than the metal itself moves, which is why miner-focused funds tend to swing harder than bullion in either direction.

"GDX did roughly three times gold's move last week ... and the juniors are more violent still," Kennedy said. "For most individual investors miners belong as a satellite position, not a core one," he added.

![hide content](https://static-redesign.cnbcfm.com/dist/a54b41835a8b60db28c2.svg)

Van Eck Gold Miners ETF five-year performance.

Cavatoni says more volatility in the price of gold could be ahead, with the upcoming Federal Reserve meeting in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, and broader policy developments helping to determine whether the rally continues.

New Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, who is communicating in a new way with the market, is a major factor. "The new Fed chairman has altered the market landscape," said Eugenia Mykuliak, founder & executive director at B2Prime Group, a brokerage platform for trading in assets including precious metals. What Mykuliak described as "cautious and often ambiguous statements" from Warsh — including at [his first Fed meeting](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/07/29/kevin-warsh-fed-treasury-yields-inflation-credibility-interest-rates.html) — hit stocks hard, and a side effect of this change in Fed leadership was that gold started to climb. When the market is unsure of the central bank's policy, money moves from stocks to safer instruments like gold and other metals.

Kennedy agreed that uncertainty about the Fed could be bullish for gold. "You have a Fed Chair signaling higher for longer into a labor market that is visibly softening. That's a stagflation setup, and gold tends to do well when the market starts questioning whether the Fed can hit both sides of its mandate," he said.

"Gold more than doubled between late 2023 and the January record, positioning got extended, and it needed to work that off," Kennedy said. It remains his view that nothing in the longer-term secular case for gold broke. "If anything the drivers accelerated. Brent is near $90 with the Strait of Hormuz still closed and Iran holding conditions on reopening it, which keeps the forward inflation risk alive even with the July print cooling," he added.

Inflation will continue to loom large in that picture, Mykuliak said, and if the market outlook remains on the side of price growth being modest, there is additional runway for gold. "It could even climb higher than the January highs," she added.

Continued buying in China and India, which remain the centers of physical gold demand, will add support to prices. Looking at the trading chart year-to-date, "the prices are at comparative lows with the potential to grow higher," Mykuliak said.

This CNBC ETF Strategist article (by Kevin Williams) analyzes the current state and future direction of the gold market in 2026. After hitting a record high above $5,300 an ounce early in 2026 (a 10-year high), gold fell by as much as 18%, but last week posted its best week since January, while gold mining stocks had their hottest five-day run since 2008. Year-to-date gold returns are now close to flat, though the metal is still up over $1,000 over the past year.

The recent rally is attributed to tamer inflation data (July CPI at 0.1% monthly, 3.4% annual, with core at 2.5%) and declining odds of a Fed rate hike, which dropped by over 20 percentage points in the past week following a soft non-farm payrolls report. The Fed has been parked at 3.50-3.75% all year, with September previously seen as "live" for a hike. Key drivers of the longer-term bull case include: fears of out-of-control U.S. fiscal spending, weak global growth, the Trump administration's expensive foreign wars and embrace of cryptocurrencies, and continued central bank gold buying (China's PBOC added 19.9 tons in July, its 21st straight month of accumulation).

Notable expert views:
- Pippa Malmgren (former Special Assistant to President George W. Bush): "Gold is the new gold" — nervous investors are turning to gold as a conservative way to preserve value amid fiscal concerns.
- Billionaire hedge fund manager John Paulson says gold is in the early stages of a long-term bull market (he has been a gold bull since 2009).
- Joe Cavatoni (World Gold Council): the recent U.S. bounce is more tactical/opportunistic, while Asian and European buying is stickier; gold is being used as a wealth preservation and portfolio diversification tool, not just a safe haven.
- Patrick Kennedy (AllSource Investment Management): his firm bought and added to GLDM off the July technical bottom; declining rate-hike expectations are not the same as a Fed positioned to cut. He notes a potential stagflation setup with a Fed signaling "higher for longer" into a softening labor market.
- Nick Cawley (Solomon Global): last week's move above the 50-day moving average and break of the lower-highs pattern should support further gains.

The article also covers gold mining stocks: many quality miners (AngloGold Ashanti, Newmont) trade at single-digit forward P/Es with strong dividends. Popular ETFs include GDX (large miners) and GDXJ (junior miners), with GDX moving roughly three times gold's move last week. ETF expense ratios noted: GLDM at 10 bps, GLD at 40 bps, IAU at 25 bps. Silver also had its best week since February.

Potential volatility lies ahead with the upcoming Jackson Hole Fed meeting and new Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, whose "cautious and often ambiguous statements" have hit stocks and boosted gold. Analysts suggest gold could even exceed January highs if inflation remains modest, supported by continued buying from China and India. Brent crude near $90 with the Strait of Hormuz closed keeps forward inflation risk alive. Kennedy advises most individual investors treat miners as a satellite position, not a core holding.

# FOMC Lowers Federal Funds Rate 25 Basis Points to 3.50%-3.75%

![](https://grea.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/12-1.png)

December 11, 2025

Share Article:

---

**FOMC Lowers Federal Funds Rate 25 Basis Points to 3.50%-3.75%**

*The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) voted at its December meeting to lower the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point to 3.50% to 3.75%, marking the third consecutive rate cut since September. One FOMC member voted to lower the target range by 1/2 percentage point, while two members preferred no change. In the December Summary of Economic Projections, Fed participants forecasted that at the end of 2026 the fed funds rate would be 3.4% and unemployment rate 4.4%, unchanged from September. The median projections for GDP rose to 2.3% and PCE inflation fell to 2.4% at the end of next year.*

“With today’s decision, we have lowered our policy rate 3/4 percentage point over our last three meetings,” said Fed Chair Jerome Powell. “This further normalization of our policy stance should help stabilize the labor market while allowing inflation to resume its downward trend toward 2% once the effects of tariffs have passed through. The adjustments to our policy stance since September bring it within a range of plausible estimates of neutral and leave us well positioned to determine the extent and timing of additional adjustments to our policy rate based on the incoming data, the evolving outlook and the balance of risks.”

**Commercial Real Estate Activity Surges in 2025**

Matt Dzbanek, Senior Director in the Capital Services Group, said he welcomed another 25 basis point cut.

“The Fed has cut rates by 175 basis points since September 2024, which has supported an accommodative interest rate environment, leading to strong acquisition and financing activity in commercial real estate throughout the year,” he said.

Nationally, commercial and multifamily mortgage loan originations surged in the third quarter of 2025, climbing 36 percent year-over-year and 18 percent from the previous quarter, according to the [Mortgage Bankers Association](https://www.mba.org/docs/default-source/research-and-forecasts/cmf-originations-index/3q25cmforiginationssurvey.pdf?sfvrsn=28aba429_1). The dollar volume of loans rose year-over-year for office (up 181%), retail (up 100%), hotels (up 66%), multifamily (up 27%) and industrial (up 5%).

Loan originations rose 83% for investor-driven lenders; 52% for depository lenders; 40% for Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac; and 5% for CMBS loans. Life company loans declined by 4%, however.

**Record Year for Capital Services Group Driven by NYC Surge and National Reach**

Fueled by robust investment sales and refinancings in New York City and across the nation, the Capital Services Group saw a record year with the dollar volume of the Group’s financing activity doubling from 2024, Dzbanek said.

New York City’s investment sales rose to $20 billion in the first nine months of the year, a 19% year-over-year increase, GREA’ New York City Q1-Q3 2025 All Asset Report shows. Multifamily sales led all asset classes with $6.6 billion in dollar volume.

Multifamily acquisitions and refinancings also dominated the Capital Services team’s pipeline this year with recent closings including:

* An $8.1 million LP & Co-GP equity package for the acquisition of a 70-unit Class-A multifamily in New Jersey.
* An $8 million bank loan with a 5.88% rate for a free market mixed-use building in Manhattan with 11 units.
* A $3,995,000 refinance loan with a 6.25% rate from a credit union for an eight-union mixed-use property in Brooklyn.
* A $3,750,000 refinance loan with a 6.13% rate from a savings bank for a 12-unit multifamily in Brooklyn.
* A $2,248,000 bank loan with a 6.60% rate for the acquisition of a 32-unit garden-style apartment building in Houston.
* A $2,065,000 refinance loan with a 5.98% rate from an agency lender for a 34-unit multifamily complex in Arkansas.

As the MBA report noted, Dzbanek said that private credit has become a large player in the New York City market. For example, a $68.1 million debt and equity package the team arranged in October to finance the acquisition and residential conversion of a Manhattan office building attracted more than two dozen term sheets from private lenders aggressively competing for the business.

New balance sheet lenders also entered the New York City market this year, targeting smaller to mid-size multifamily buildings with solid fundamentals.

**Market Entering New Year Positioned for Growth**

The commercial real estate market showed exceptional resilience in 2025, driven by increased investment activity and mortgage originations.

Looking ahead, the national multifamily sector will see increased liquidity in 2026, thanks to the Federal Housing Finance Agency boosting Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac loan purchase caps to $88 billion apiece for a total of $176 billion, up from $146 billion in 2025.p>

The market is entering the new year positioned for continued momentum and strong transactional activity.
