<webpage_content>
# Gold Watch - Impact of the Ukraine war on gold prices

PublicationNatural resources

Gold prices have rallied by 10% since the end of January. The rally reflects inflation fears, the war and concerns about currency debasement. However, gold’s behaviour as safe haven is erratic. Inflation fears could continue to support gold prices, but market panic could send prices lower. We expect volatile gold prices. Our new forecasts for end 2022 and 2023 are USD 2,000 per ounce

[220310 - Gold Watch.pdf692 KB](https://assets.ctfassets.net/1u811bvgvthc/4oCewXVkEDPOiaseo7IoGX/c96e1d84730a60f142b051229d9b1560/220310_-_Gold_Watch.pdf)

[![Georgette Boele](https://images.ctfassets.net/1u811bvgvthc/5lPknbBxpxhHYb3wzzFtwS/da046257dc19afd0af3b458ccabaa070/Georgette_Boele.jpg?w=200)

Georgette Boele

Senior FX & Oil Strategist](/research/en/our-research/georgette-boele)

#### Introduction

Gold prices had a weak start to the year as rate hike expectations increased (in the US and other countries), US real yields rose (less negative), and the US dollar performed well. However, when the tensions between Russia and Ukraine became to the fore, these earlier mentioned drivers slowly but surely lost their influence on gold prices. Gold prices started to bounce higher. Since the end of January, gold prices have rallied by 10%. When Russia invaded Ukraine, higher oil, gas, wheat and other commodity prices triggered a considerable rise in inflation expectations. These expectations have outpaced the rise in nominal yields resulting in lower real yields in the major economies. This has supported gold prices.

But there is more. Gold has started to behave like a safe haven asset again. It now has a positive relationship with US equity market volatility and the US dollar. We have held the view that gold’s safe haven appeal is erratic and not stable and that there are periods that it behaves like a safe haven and other periods like a risk asset (more on this below). As is the case with a number of other commodities, gold’s fortunes have changed for the better as result of the war in Ukraine. In this report we will look at the demand and supply side dynamics. We will also present our new gold price outlook.

#### Have demand side dynamics dominated the direction in the gold market?

Gold is like no other commodity. It has unique supply and demand features that make gold unique in commodity markets. It is used to store value, used for transactions, but also as speculation. It has all these different features and therefore different types of investors are interested in gold. The first type of investors use gold to store value or as wealth preservation. Central banks buy gold to diversify their reserves. Central banks’ gold reserves have increased, and they are at the level of the 90s (see the graph on the left below). Also, the People’s Bank of China and the Russian central bank (see graph on the right below) bought gold. But in recent years they stopped doing so.

Not only central banks have bought gold to store value and as wealth preservation, investors have also done so. They have the tendency to buy gold if they fear inflation, if there are geopolitical fears or increased tensions or even a war. If they fear inflation, they think that central banks will not tighten monetary policy fast enough to counter inflation. Then inflation expectations will rise at a faster pace than nominal yields. As a result, real yields will decline. Gold is an asset that doesn’t pay a coupon or dividend, but it is not declining when inflation expectations rise (see graph on the left below).

On 8 February real yields in the major economies peaked. Since then, real yields in the major economies have dropped substantially (becoming more negative) mainly because of a substantial rise in inflation expectations. Higher energy and wheat and other commodity prices have only accelerated the move.If investors fear a war or severe stress, they also prefer gold. These investors often buy physical gold like coins or bars, or futures that could deliver physical gold. There is increased interest in gold on the futures markets. Investors have increased their long positions in gold with the possibility of physical delivery (see graph on the right below). These positions are large but not excessive.

Next to being used as a way to store value, gold (and silver) could also be used in transactions to buy goods. In this sense, it has some features of a currency like the US dollar or the euro. If consumers and/or investors are expecting or are confronted with a debasement of their own currencies, they could buy gold in order to be able to buy goods – though it is worth noting that gold payments are not widely accepted. We have experienced this behaviour during the sharp depreciation of the Turkish lira, but debasement of the Russian ruble and sanctions on Russian assets could also have triggered demand for gold as transaction unit.

Finally, investors could use gold to speculate. Since 2004 this has become increasingly popular. The sharp rise in outstanding ETF positions has also resulted in a rise in gold prices and vise versa. So gold prices have become more volatile as it opened to a large group of investors. Products such as ETFs, metal-account gold make it easier to profit from movements in the gold price without holding the physical gold on your own name. Some of the funds have bought the physical gold but this will generally not be on a name of a certain investor that bought an ETF. In short, this is not the way of investing to own physical gold on your name in the end. Investors that want to profit from volatility in the gold price driven by dynamics in the dollar, expectations about central banks and other financial factors are often attracted to this way of investing. As mentioned before, gold doesn’t pay a coupon or dividend. When investors expect central banks to ease and yields to decline, gold as an investment asset is attractive. If is in this environment equity markets rise and equity market volatility declines, gold tends to move in the opposite direction as equity market volatility. As a result, it behaves as a risk-on asset. When investors expect central banks to tighten policy and rates rise, gold as an investment asset is not attractive. So, when yields rise, often gold prices decline and vice versa. Next to that higher US dollar is generally not gold for gold prices.

As positions in these products have grown very large, the behaviour of these investors has more and more dominated the direction in gold prices. As a result, the effect of the gold buying driven by the storage and the transaction arguments has been overshadowed by the speculation of investors. So over time gold has become less of a safe haven asset and more a risk-on asset and gold’s safe haven appeal is erratic and not stable.

What driver has resulted in the substantial rise in gold prices? Since 8 February the relationship between gold prices and the VIX has turned positive (higher equity market volatility, higher gold prices) and the relationship between gold and real yields have remained negative (lower real yields higher gold prices). Next to that the positions in ETF have increased but not enough to justify the large rise in gold prices. This points into the direction that investors have bought gold as a store of value and probably also as transaction unit. They fear inflation and the war and the currency debasement and favour physical gold.

#### What about supply?

On 7 March, the London Bullion Market Association (LBMA) suspended all six Russian gold refineries from its Good Delivery List, meaning their newly minted bars (cut from a rolled strip of gold) can no longer trade in the London market. London is the biggest marketplace for gold in world by volume of trade. Could this result in shortage in the gold market? In our opinion not. First, the supply side of the gold is very fragmentated. A lot of countries mine and export gold and there is no monopolistic or oligopolistic market structure. China is the largest gold miner with 12% of the world supply, next comes Russia with 10% (see graph on the left below). So, this is a completely different picture than for palladium where both Russia and South Africa are responsible for around 40% of supply; they hold together 80%. Second, the aboveground stocks in gold in the form of jewellery are enormous (see graph on the right below). At the end of 2021 total above ground stocks stood at 203,000 tonnes while annual mine supply is around 3,300 tonnes. Therefore, it is very unlikely that the gold market will experience a shortage. Of course, the price needs to be attractive enough for the holders of gold jewellery to sell. So, the price could still rise. Even though we think ta global shortage is unlikely, there could be a temporary shortage in a certain location/country.

#### Our gold price outlook

We have recently changed our view on macro-economy ([see Russia-Ukraine: Sanctions trigger a lasting trade re-alignment)](https://www.abnamro.com/research/en/our-research/russia-ukraine-sanctions-to-trigger-a-lasting-trade-re-alignment). We now expect that supply disruptions due to sanctions or self-sanctioning will cover oil and some other non-energy commodities, and will last for around a year, as non-Russian sources of supply are secured. We expect that consumer price inflation more broadly will spike further, weighing on confidence and consumption. We think that growth will be weaker, inflation will be higher and central banks will react differently to these new challenges. While a delay to ECB tightening and potentially a continuation of asset purchases is looking more likely, we do not foresee a significant easing in policy of the kind we witnessed during the pandemic. For the Fed, given that the US economy will be facing higher inflation but less of a growth hit (as it is much less dependent on Russian commodity imports), the calculus shifts even more in favour of rate hikes. As a result of this new outlook, we expect that real yields to remain under pressure. In addition, we expect a risk off environment in markets and a higher US dollar due to safe haven demand.

What is the impact on gold prices? We expect that gold prices are supported in the current environment but that there also will be a lot of price volatility. Reasons behind this view are as follow. Higher inflation expectations and lower real yields are positive for gold as mentioned above. So, investors will continue to buy gold as an inflation hedge. But as the Fed will continue to hike and we also expect a higher dollar, gold’s fortunes will mainly be positive versus other currencies than the dollar. They will likely prefer physical gold to non-physical gold. But severe risk off and even market panic is usually not a positive environment for gold prices (remember the aggressive sell-off during the covid panic in March 2020). When there is market panic, investors liquidate most positions and buy the most liquid assets such as US Treasuries, the US dollar and the Japanese yen. They will likely also sell speculative gold positions such as ETFs and other instruments and these positions are extremely large.

Meanwhile some investors will continue to buy physical gold or gold positions with physical delivery for storage and transaction argument. It is likely that the impact of the position liquidation of the speculative gold positions is larger than the physical buying of the other investors. Despite lower gold prices, the premium between physical gold and non-physical gold is expected to increase. Finally, we think that a shortage in the gold market is very unlikely, so runaway prices like seen in other commodities is unlikely in the gold market in our view.

Taken all together we expect price volatility in the gold market and our new gold price forecasts for the end of 2022 and the end of 2023 stands at USD 2,000 per ounce.

--- SOURCE 1: [PDF] Federal Reserve issues FOMC statement ---
URL: https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/files/monetary20260729a1.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On July 29, 2026, the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) voted 9-3 to maintain the federal funds rate target range at 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent, in support of the Federal Reserve's dual mandate. The Committee continues its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system. The statement notes that economic activity is expanding at a solid pace despite elevated uncertainty partly due to the Middle East conflict, with strong productivity growth and capital investment. Job gains have kept pace with the workforce and the unemployment rate has changed little, though inflation remains elevated relative to the 2 percent goal, partly reflecting supply shocks that have driven up prices in certain sectors including energy. The Committee affirmed it will deliver price stability.

Voting against the action were Beth M. Hammack, Neel Kashkari, and Lorie K. Logan, who preferred to raise the target range by 1/4 percentage point at this meeting.

In implementing the monetary policy stance (effective July 30, 2026):
• The Board of Governors voted unanimously to maintain the interest rate paid on reserve balances at 3.65 percent.
• The FOMC directed the Open Market Desk to maintain the federal funds rate in the 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent range; conduct standing overnight repurchase agreement operations at 3.75 percent; conduct standing overnight reverse repurchase agreement operations at 3.5 percent with a per-counterparty limit of $160 billion per day; purchase Treasury bills and other short-term Treasury securities as needed to maintain ample reserves; roll over principal payments from Treasury securities holdings; and reinvest principal payments from agency securities into Treasury bills.
• The Board of Governors voted unanimously to establish the primary credit rate at the existing level of 3.75 percent.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 2: August 2026 Fed & Rates Call Update ---
URL: https://www.mufgresearch.com/rates/august-2026-fed-rates-call-update

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a MUFG (Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group) research note published August 20, 2026, by analysts George Goncalves and Agron Nicaj, updating their Federal Reserve and US rates forecast. The core thesis is that the Fed will remain on hold for the balance of 2026 (no hikes and no cuts), pushing easing expectations into early 2027.

Key points:
1. The authors do not see urgency to restart rate hikes and expect the Fed to remain on hold through 2026.
2. They have pushed back their easing expectations into early 2027.
3. Each tenor point estimate was revised higher by 25-50bps across the forecast horizon.
4. They argue the US rates market is in an "overshoot mode" that is creating value in the bond market.

Macro rationale: Data has looked notably weaker since the last FOMC meeting, with both nonfarm payrolls (NFP) and retail sales growth negative in July. While core CPI rebounded in July after a weak June (inflation hasn't eased enough to fully dissuade hawks), wage growth has fallen to levels consistent with 2% inflation, with little added thrust from tariffs and energy prices going forward.

Markets perspective: Rate hike expectations have declined while long-term rates have meaningfully increased, "doing some of the tightening for the Fed." The authors do not see inflationary pressures re-surfacing strongly enough to warrant immediate hikes, noting this is largely a supply shock environment.

Fed rate path implications: Hawkish tension at the Fed will keep near-term rate hike expectations priced-in but not delivered. Rate hike expectations won't fully fade until resolution of the US/Iran war or a material drop in inflation; they will trade in a 30-60% probability range of a 25bp hike at each upcoming FOMC meeting. As 2027 approaches, markets are expected to pivot back to pricing in cuts.

Forecast table (Q3-2026 through Q2-2027):
- Fed Funds Rate: 3.625 → 3.625 → 3.375 → 3.125
- US 2-Year: 4.125 → 3.875 → 3.625 → 3.500
- US 5-Year: 4.250 → 4.125 → 3.875 → 3.750
- US 10-Year: 4.500 → 4.375 → 4.250 → 4.125
- US 30-Year: 5.000 → 4.875 → 4.625 → 4.500

The authors maintain a checklist heading into the Jackson Hole Symposium and September FOMC meeting to steer their Fed view. The website includes disclaimers that materials are produced only for professional investors, are not investment research or investment advice.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 4: Fed meeting recap: July 2026 ---
URL: https://www.cnbc.com/2026/07/29/fed-meeting-today-live-updates.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a CNBC live blog covering the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) decision and Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh's news conference on Wednesday, July 29, 2026.

**Key Decision:** The Fed kept its benchmark interest rate unchanged at 3.5% to 3.75%. Three policymakers dissented in favor of a rate hike—Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan, Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, and Minneapolis Fed President Neel Kashkari—marking the first time since September 2016 that three voters dissented. Governor Christopher Waller also made statements supportive of tighter policy.

**Warsh's Comments:** Warsh said the Fed "will not hesitate to act" to meet its 2% inflation goal but declined to provide forward guidance or hints on rate policy. He insisted the decision was not a "pause" but "a rigorous review of the economic situation." He acknowledged a "good family fight" over the decision and reiterated: "We will deliver price stability." Warsh noted the Fed "doesn't always need to be the center of attention" and welcomed markets reacting to real data. He confirmed press conferences will continue for 2026 and said his Jackson Hole keynote speech (Aug. 27-29) is currently "a blank piece of paper" but may be informed by the five policy task forces he created.

**Market Reaction:** Stocks fell after the decision (S&P 500 down 0.6%, Nasdaq down 0.5%, Dow down ~840 points/1.6%). The 30-year Treasury yield topped 5.2%, the highest since 2007, while the 10-year yield rose above 7 basis points to 4.677%. Bond yields jumped following the meeting despite the hold.

**Inflation Context:** June CPI posted a surprise 0.4% drop, but the Middle East conflict (U.S. vs. Iran) has reversed the decline in gas prices. Brent crude jumped more than 15% month-to-date in July and more than 38% in 2026 due to Strait of Hormuz disruptions. The average gallon of unleaded gas hit $4.09, up 6% from a month ago.

**Expert Reactions:**
- President Trump claimed Warsh "would love to see lower interest rates" but is held back by a "political board."
- Indeed economist Aubrey Woessner said the labor market is "playing second fiddle" to inflation.
- Vanguard's Adam Schickling expects rate hikes to be "difficult this year" due to a cooling labor market.
- Goldman Sachs' Kay Haigh said a September hike is "finely balanced," dependent on Middle East developments and the next two CPI prints.
- Thornburg's Christian Hoffmann called it an "uncomfortable hold."
- FWDBONDS' Chris Rupkey criticized the Fed for showing "no sign of taking steps" to control inflation.
- Citadel Securities expected a surprise hike; Fundstrat's Tom Lee expected a hold.
- Former Fed Governor Stephen Miran said rates should stay on hold, viewing current inflation as "transitory" and driven by temporary war effects.

**Other Notes:** Wall Street is adjusting to the "Warsh era" of less communication—F/m Investments launched "WarshGPT," an AI bot to interpret Warsh. Fed CEO Hassett said Warsh's stewardship is "already a home run." Federal Reserve Governor Stephen Miran (served Sept 2025–May 2026) argued for holding rates.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"I understand the desire for rolling forecasts and commentary from this committee, but for our part, we need to observe market reaction to developments direct and unfiltered. I want to stress, of course, that decisions by this committee matter a great deal, and where necessary and appropriate, we will not hesitate to act." — Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh
</key_excerpts>

This article from ISA Bullion (published May 29, 2026) examines how central bank gold buying is reshaping the gold market and driving prices to historic highs. Gold reached an all-time high of $5,589.38 per ounce on January 28, 2026, part of a structural shift that began in 2022.

Key statistics and facts:
- Central banks purchased 863 tonnes of gold in 2025, nearly double the pre-2022 annual average of 400-500 tonnes, though below the record 1,000+ tonne pace of 2022-2024
- More than 22 institutions reported meaningful gold reserve increases in 2025; Poland led with 102 tonnes (total reserves: 550 tonnes); Kazakhstan set a record; Brazil re-entered after a four-year absence

How central bank buying impacts prices (four mechanisms):
1. Creates a price floor (currently ~$4,500-4,600/oz where sovereign buying intensifies) - central banks buy as policy, not trade
2. Reduces available supply to institutional and retail investors
3. Shifts market psychology - validates gold as premier store of value
4. Amplifies other demand drivers (ETF inflows, retail demand, weakening dollar)

Root causes: Russia's ~$300 billion in frozen reserves in 2022 served as a wake-up call (gold cannot be frozen), accelerating de-dollarisation. Persistent inflation, geopolitical tension, and trade uncertainty also support the case. In the World Gold Council's 2025 survey, 95% of central banks expected global gold holdings to increase; none expected a decline.

Price forecasts: ING forecasts gold averaging $4,325/oz in 2026; J.P. Morgan sees potential $5,000/oz by Q4 2026; State Street puts 30% probability on $5,000 in 2026.

FAQ highlights: Poland, China, India, Kazakhstan, and Brazil are the most active buyers (China, India, and Turkey accounted for ~42% of 2025 central bank purchases); coordinated large-scale selling (like the 1990s G10 agreement) has not been signalled, so downside risk is limited; retail investors are advised to use dollar-cost averaging into physical gold to position alongside institutional demand.

Switzerland, India, and Japan hold several hundred tonnes each.

The article notes short-term uncertainty: the Middle East war may have forced some states to sell gold to shore up foreign exchange reserves amid elevated oil prices, and some analysts warn volatility could persist, testing central banks' appetite for continued accumulation. <summary>
This article from Bullion Trading LLC analyzes the 2026 gold and silver market correction following a record January rally, arguing that the pullback is normal behavior for a healthy bull market rather than a sign of a fundamental decline.

**What Happened in January 2026:** Gold reached an intraday record of $5,602 per ounce on January 29, 2026, a gain of 29.5% for the month, and had more than doubled since the start of 2025. Silver touched an all-time high above $121 per ounce, surging roughly 68.5% in January and more than 300% from its starting point near $24 at the beginning of 2025. The rallies were driven by central bank buying, geopolitical uncertainty, currency debasement concerns, and speculative capital.

**The Correction:** On January 30, President Trump nominated Kevin Warsh (an inflation hawk) as the next Federal Reserve Chair, causing markets to reprice interest rate expectations. Gold plunged $380 in just 28 minutes, declining about 10% from its high. Silver dropped more than 30% in just over a week. As of early March 2026, gold was trading around $5,088 per ounce (about 9% below its peak but still more than double its start-of-2025 price), and silver was near $82 per ounce (down about 32% from its record).

**Historical Context:** The article compares this correction to the January 1980 silver parabolic rally to $50 (followed by a 50%+ loss) and the April 2011 silver run to $49.51 (followed by a ~35% pullback). The 1970s bull market featured five corrections exceeding 20%, and the 2001-2011 bull market saw pullbacks of 15-34%, yet overall trends remained decisively higher.

**Why Silver Falls Harder:** Silver's market is much smaller than gold's, requiring less capital to move prices, making it more volatile in both directions. Industrial demand accounts for 59% of silver usage, with solar photovoltaic demand representing 17% of total silver demand (up from 5.6% in 2015). The silver market has run structural supply deficits for seven consecutive years.

**Fundamentals Unchanged:** Central banks continue buying gold (248.6 tonnes purchased in Q1 2025, the highest quarterly total ever recorded). J.P. Morgan analysts noted gold has surged over 170% in five years, citing geopolitical volatility and fragmentation as key drivers. ANZ Bank forecasts gold reaching $5,800 per ounce in Q2 2026.

## Gold Mid-Year Outlook 2026: Point break (World Gold Council)

**Publication details:** Report by Juan Carlos Artigas, Taylor Burnette, and Dr. Fergal O'Connor, published July 2026 by the World Gold Council. Data as of 26 June 2026.

**Executive Summary:**
- Gold soared to record highs in January 2026, crossing above US$5,500/oz intraday (spot high of US$5,595.47 on 29 January), before dipping below US$4,000/oz in late June (spot low of US$3,959.33 on 24 June; LBMA PM low of US$4,001.80 on 25 June).
- Gold is down about 7% year-to-date but remains among the top performers over the past year.
- The H1 rollercoaster was driven by heightened geopolitical risks (US–Iran conflict), elevated options activity, and abrupt shifts in investor sentiment.
- Realized volatility spiked above 50% during the US–Iran conflict, then subsided below 30%, though still above the 20-year average of 17%.
- Asian markets are playing a growing role in gold price discovery—the bulk of gold's pullbacks occurred during US trading hours, while rebounds generally occurred during Asian hours.

**Current Valuation and H2 Outlook:**
- At current levels (~US$4,100/oz), gold's price is broadly in line with macro consensus expectations (moderate growth, cooling but elevated inflation, expectations of limited central bank tightening).
- If current conditions don't materially change, gold may trade ±5% around US$4,100/oz during H2 2026.
- Gold could resume an upward trend around US$4,500/oz, with a strong, clear signal potentially pushing it sustainably toward US$5,000/oz.
- Downside scenario: if gold fell 10%–15% from current levels, further downside would likely be limited due to bargain-hunting demand.

**Key Drivers (Gold Return Attribution Model - GRAM for H1):**
- Momentum: 24% of variability
- Risk & uncertainty: 17%
- Opportunity cost (FX): 14%
- Economic expansion: 12%
- Opportunity cost (Rates): 3%
- Total explained: 70%; other factors: 30%

**Upside Catalysts:**
1. Worsening economic or geopolitical conditions
2. Reversal in interest-rate expectations
3. Long-term investor participation

**Key Macro Context:**
- Market expects the Fed, Bank of England, Bank of Japan, and ECB to raise policy rates before year-end (Fed hike by October).
- Global economy expected to grow 2.9% y/y in 2026; US at 2.1% y/y.
- US inflation expected to peak near 3.9% in Q2; global inflation averaging 4.3% for the year.
- November 2026 US midterm elections could increase policy uncertainty (Democrats positioned to regain House; Senate may stay Republican).
- Rate hike expectations have tempered stock market momentum; private credit market concerns noted.

**Downside Risks:**
- US dollar strength and rates rising beyond expectations
- Investor risk-on sentiment
- Technical factors (gold below ~US$3,860/oz could trigger additional downside)
- Gold is ~25% below its record high

**Historical Drawdown Analysis (since 1971):**
- Drawdowns of 5%+: 29 occurrences, avg 16%, median 8%
- Drawdowns of 10%+: 11 occurrences, avg 30%, median 28%
- Drawdowns of 20%+: 8 occurrences, avg 36%, median 29%

**Beyond Macro Factors:**

*Central Banks:*
- Bought an average of 1,000t per year since 2022; some tactically sold/swapped gold in Q1 2026.
- An additional 20t–30t increase in reserves above the ~600t/year long-term average should translate to ~1% increase in gold price.

*India:*
- Gold's second-largest market with ~800t/year net demand.
- Due to US–Iran conflict pressure on INR and current account deficit, India raised import duty from 6% to 15% since early April.
- Estimated import duty increases alone will reduce jewellery, bar and coin demand by 50t–60t (~10% y/y).

**Gold Price Sensitivity (Table 4, all else equal):**
- Central banks: directly proportional; +20t–30t = +1% price
- Indian import duty: inversely proportional; +10% duty = -2% price
- Interest rates: inversely proportional; 25bp decrease in US 10y yield = +1.75% price
- Inflation: directly proportional; +1% CPI = +0.5% price
- Geopolitical risk: directly proportional; +100pt GPR/month = +2.5% price

--- SOURCE 10: Federal Reserve ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The Federal Reserve System (the Fed) is the central banking system of the United States, established on December 23, 1913, through the Federal Reserve Act following a series of financial panics (especially the severe 1907 crisis) that created a desire for central control of the American monetary system. Although an instrument of the U.S. government, the Fed is considered an independent central bank due to its structural insulation from political interference. Events such as the Great Depression and the Great Recession have expanded its remit over the years.

Congress established three key objectives for monetary policy: maximizing employment, stabilizing prices (interpreted as an average inflation rate of 2 percent per year), and moderating long-term interest rates (the first two comprise the "dual mandate"). Its duties also include supervising and regulating banks, maintaining financial system stability, and providing financial services to depository institutions, the U.S. government, and foreign official institutions. The Fed also conducts economic research and publishes the Beige Book and the FRED database.

The system is multi-layered: governed by the presidentially appointed Board of Governors (FRB) in Washington, D.C., with twelve regional Federal Reserve Banks regulating and overseeing privately owned commercial banks. The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) sets monetary policy by adjusting the target federal funds rate. Key current leadership includes Chair Kevin Warsh, Vice Chair Philip Jefferson, and Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman. Current rates: bank rate 3.75%, interest rate target 3.50–3.75%, interest on reserves 3.65%; reserve requirements are now none.

Purposes include addressing banking panics, serving as central bank, balancing private interests of banks with centralized government responsibility, supervising banking institutions, protecting consumer credit rights, conducting monetary policy, maintaining financial system stability, and providing financial services. The Fed operates under a fractional-reserve banking system and serves as lender of last resort. It was designed as a compromise between privatized and government-regulated banking philosophies—agrarian/progressive interests (led by William Jennings Bryan) favored public control while the nation's bankers opposed political appointees, resulting in a hybrid public-private, centralized-decentralized structure.

As the government's bank, the Fed processes trillions in financial transactions, handles Treasury checking accounts and federal tax deposits, issues currency (the Bureau of Engraving and Printing delivered 57.95 billion notes in FY2020 at 7.4 cents per note), and sells/redeems U.S. government securities. The Board supervises approximately 900 state member banks and 5,000 bank holding companies, oversees consumer protection laws (Truth in Lending, Equal Credit Opportunity, Home Mortgage Disclosure Acts), and can be audited by the Government Accountability Office (GAO) through the 1978 Federal Banking Agency Audit Act. The Fed's monetary policy tools include the federal funds rate, interest on reserve balances, open market operations, discount window, term deposit facility, and quantitative easing. Historical crisis tools include reserve requirements (since expired) and crisis facilities from 2008 (term auction facility, commercial paper funding facility, etc.). The Fed has faced criticism over inflation management, transparency, and its role in economic downturns, with some calling for its abolition.

URL: https://bullionexchanges.com/blog/gold-and-silver-lease-rates-2026-why-markets-are-tight

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Bullion Exchanges (published February 23, 2026) examines why gold and silver lease rates - the annualized cost to borrow physical bullion in wholesale markets like LBMA and COMEX - are elevated in 2026, signaling tighter deliverable supply rather than depletion of global inventories.

Key data points:
- Gold spot price trading above $5,000/oz; silver near mid-$80s/oz
- Gold lease rates: 1.0%-2.0% annualized depending on tenor
- Silver lease rates: 6%-7%+ in short tenors, with brief February spikes

Gold lease rate drivers: central bank accumulation reducing floating inventory, ETF/institutional inflows removing metal from lending, macro risk hedging, and collateral preference (institutions holding gold outright rather than leasing for minimal yield).

Silver lease rate drivers (more volatile than gold): industrial demand surge (solar panels, EV components, electronics), persistent structural supply deficits, inventory migration between London and COMEX vault systems creating localized scarcity, backwardation signals (immediate delivery prices above futures), and speculative/ETF flows. Silver's smaller, thinner wholesale market makes it inherently more sensitive to demand surges.

Supply chain components: form mismatch (institutional bars vs. retail products), geographic mismatch (metal in London vs. demand in New York/Asia), refining bottlenecks from scrap flow surges, and transportation/settlement delays - all contributing to elevated lease rates.

Historical perspective: lease rate spikes occurred during the 1980 Hunt Brothers silver crisis, 2008 financial crisis, 2020 pandemic (London-New York dislocations), and 2025 trade/tariff volatility (silver spikes exceeding 20%-30% annualized). Compared to these episodes, 2026 rates are orderly and far below systemic crisis levels.

Investor takeaways: elevated lease rates indicate strong physical demand and localized tightness, not scarcity. Gold leasing remains stable/controlled; silver leasing is tighter due to industrial factors. Markets historically rebalance over time. The article includes FAQs covering lease rate definitions, why silver rates exceed gold, backwardation, and investor implications.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 4: Silver Shortage Signals: COMEX and LBMA Vault Risks in 2026 ---
URL: https://www.nycbullion.com/blog/post/silver-shortage-signals-comex-vs-lbma-inventory-clues.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This NYC Bullion blog article examines silver shortage signals by analyzing inventory data from COMEX (futures market) and LBMA (London wholesale vaults). 

Key points:
- Silver differs from gold as it trades as both a monetary metal and industrial material (used in solar panels, electronics, EVs, medical devices, defense, and emerging tech).
- COMEX inventory is split into "registered" (metal with warrants attached, deliverable against futures) and "eligible" (meets exchange standards but no active warrant, not automatically deliverable). The registered/eligible ratio is central to assessing delivery readiness.
- LBMA provides monthly data on total London vault holdings but does not divide into registered/eligible categories and does not show immediately available metal.
- COMEX and LBMA answer different questions—COMEX for delivery mechanics, LBMA for wholesale inventory trends—and should not be treated as competing truth sources.
- No single indicator proves a shortage. A serious warning sign requires confirmation from multiple signals: falling COMEX registered stocks, declining LBMA holdings, rising delivery demand, stronger physical premiums, ETF outflows, elevated lease rates, and persistent global deficits.
- Silver supply is constrained: mine supply responds slowly to prices (much is mined as a byproduct of copper, lead, zinc, and gold), and global supply has struggled to keep pace with demand.
- Demand drivers include solar energy, electronics, automotive, AI infrastructure, 5G, medical equipment, defense, plus investment demand from coins, bars, rounds, and ETFs.
- Retail availability is separate from wholesale vault data—coins and bars require fabrication, so premiums and delivery delays can rise even when wholesale bars remain plentiful.
- Bullion buyers should watch product premiums, delivery times, mint supply, dealer inventories, and buyback spreads alongside vault data.
- Silver shortages can be localized; the market is connected but not perfectly uniform.

The article includes a detailed FAQ section covering what shortage signals are, definitions of COMEX registered/eligible silver, the registered-to-eligible ratio, LBMA vs COMEX differences, whether falling registered silver proves a shortage, why retail silver can seem scarce despite high vault inventories, the role of industrial demand, and which indicator is most important.

The article was published June 10, 2026, and includes related blog links on inflation's effect on precious metals, .999 vs .9999 gold purity, platinum's relationship with gold, and online bullion dealer comparisons.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Registered silver is metal stored in approved warehouses with warrants attached, making it available for delivery against futures contracts. Eligible silver meets exchange standards and sits in approved warehouses, but it does not have an active warrant attached. In simple terms, registered silver is deliverable; eligible silver is stored but not automatically available for futures delivery."

--- SOURCE 1: Fed Cuts Rates and Signals More to Come in 2025 | Morningstar ---
URL: https://www.morningstar.com/economy/fed-cuts-rates-signals-more-come-2025

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The Federal Reserve cut the federal-funds rate by 0.25 percentage points to a target range of 4.00%-4.25%, a move widely expected since the August jobs report showed sharp deterioration in job growth. The central bank's press release noted the committee "judges that downside risks to employment have risen."

The cut was not unanimous—11 of 12 FOMC members voted for a quarter-point cut, with Stephen Miran being the lone voter for a half-point cut. Miran, recently confirmed to the Board of Governors after serving as chair of the Council of Economic Advisers in the Trump administration, likely accounts for the dot plot projection of a 2.75%-3.00% rate by end of 2025 (another 1.25 points in cuts). His advocacy for looser policy aligns with President Trump's desires, though he doesn't endorse Trump's stated goal of a 1.25%-1.50% range. Miran's term runs through January 2026, and a reappointment could give him a fresh 14-year term. Fed Chair Jerome Powell affirmed that independence is "deeply in [the Federal Reserve's] culture."

The broader FOMC projections show a median expectation of 3.50%-3.75% by end of 2025 (in line with market expectations) and 3.25%-3.50% by end of 2026 (only one 0.25-point cut in 2026, while the market expected 0.75 points). Morningstar is in between, expecting 3.00%-3.25% at end of 2026.

On economic projections, the FOMC expects core inflation at 2.6% year-over-year by end of 2026, while Morningstar expects 3.2% due to tariffs. The FOMC projects unemployment at 4.4% in Q4 2026 vs. Morningstar's 4.7%, and GDP growth at 1.6% vs. Morningstar's 1.3%. Given that inflationary effects from tariffs are expected to be a one-off shock counterbalanced by increasing economic slack, labor market risks call for looser monetary policy.

Powell described a labor market in a state of precarious balance, noting unemployment has averaged 4.2% over the past three months vs. 4.1% in Q1 2025. Both labor supply and demand have fallen; if demand keeps contracting, the economy risks a vicious cycle of layoffs and spending contraction.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Congressional Research Service (CRS) Insight report (IN12635) titled "Federal Reserve Cuts Interest Rates in Late 2025," authored by Marc Labonte and published on December 22, 2025. The report analyzes the Federal Reserve's decision to reduce the federal funds rate (FFR) in the final quarter of 2025, framed within the Fed's dual mandate of maximum employment and price stability (2% inflation target).

Key events in chronological order:
- 2020: Fed reduced rates to zero in response to COVID-19
- 2022-2023: Fed raised rates to a peak range of 5%-5.25% in response to high inflation
- September-December 2024: Fed reduced rates three times toward a more neutral level
- 2024 through September 2025: Fed held FFR unchanged, waiting to see how President Trump's 2025 tariffs would affect inflation versus employment
- September through December 2025: Fed made rate cuts at its three final meetings of 2025

- The Fed justified rate cuts citing "downside risks to employment rose in recent months." Monthly job growth was below average from May to September 2025, and the unemployment rate rose about one percentage point since mid-2023 and half a percentage point since early 2025.

- Gold was trading near $4,356, down ~1.2% from a two-month high of $4,450 set the prior day.
- Two consecutive months of cooling inflation drove September Fed rate-hike odds sharply lower: July PPI was flat month-over-month (well below 0.2% consensus), and July CPI rose just 0.1% month-over-month.
- CME FedWatch implied probability of a September rate hike fell from ~54% a week earlier to ~39% on August 13 (it had been 46% after the July 29 FOMC meeting).
- Lower rate-hike expectations compress real yields, reducing the opportunity cost of holding gold and pushing prices higher—the mechanism that drove gold above its 100-day moving average at $4,387 for the first time in over two months.

**The Jackson Hole significance:**
- The symposium runs August 27–29, 2026. Warsh will speak as Fed Chair for the first time since taking office on May 22, 2026.

**Structural/fiscal context:**
- US public debt stands at ~$39.89 trillion; CBO projects net interest payments of ~$1.0 trillion in FY2026, matching the base defense appropriation for the first time. Every 25 bps rate increase adds tens of billions to that annual cost.
- Central banks purchased 288.9 tonnes of gold in Q2 2026, up 62% year-over-year and the strongest second quarter on record (World Gold Council), buying even as gold prices were falling.
- Physical gold carries no credit risk and pays no interest, sitting outside the fiscal trap the Fed is navigating.

**Levels/events to watch:**
- University of Michigan inflation expectations survey on August 14 and July PCE release in late August will shape the hawks' case.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Chicago Fed Letter (No. 464, November 2021) by Robert Barsky, Craig Epstein, Adrian Lafont-Mueller, and Younggeun Yoo examines what drives gold prices since the U.S. dollar price of gold was allowed to float freely in 1971. The article identifies three key drivers commonly cited: inflationary expectations, real interest rates, and pessimism about future macroeconomic conditions. The authors organize their empirical evidence around three claims: gold is a hedge against inflation, gold is sensitive to expected long-term real interest rates, and gold is seen as protective against "bad economic times."

Using multiple regression analyses across three specifications — annual levels (1971–2019), quarterly innovations (VAR), and daily differences (2003–2021) — the authors find:
- In the annual levels regression, a 1 percentage point rise in long-term real interest rates lowers real gold prices by 13.1%, while an extra percentage point of ten-year expected inflation raises real gold prices by 37%. Real world GDP has a coefficient of 1.125, and a one standard deviation increase (8.1 points) in pessimistic survey responses raises gold prices by 9.7%.
- In the quarterly innovations regression, a 1 percentage point innovation in expected ten-year real interest rates is associated with a 3.4% reduction in real gold prices, while innovations in PTR (inflation expectations) play no significant role. A 10 percentage point innovation in pessimistic expectations raises real gold prices by 5%.
- In the daily regression using TIPS yields, a 1 percentage point change in TIPS yield lowers gold prices by 1.1%, while a 1 percentage point change in break-even inflation raises prices by 2.7%.

Key findings: The negative effect of real interest rates on gold prices predicted by theory holds in all three contexts. Two of three specifications support the inflation hedge view, with the inflation effect quantitatively larger than the real interest rate effect. In the early part of the sample (1971–2000), variation in inflation or inflationary expectations was the single most important driver; from 2001 onward, long-term real interest rates and pessimism about future economic activity became dominant. During 2001–2012, the long-term real interest rate fell about 400 basis points while real gold prices rose more than fivefold. The authors conclude that disinflation since 2001 might have been expected to produce low gold prices, but any such effect was more than offset by unprecedentedly low long-term real interest rates and pessimism about economic activity.

--- SOURCE 2: How Fed Funds Rate Hikes Influence Gold Prices - Investopedia ---
URL: https://www.investopedia.com/articles/investing/100915/effect-fed-fund-rate-hikes-gold.asp

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Investopedia article examines the relationship between Federal Reserve interest rate hikes and gold prices. The article challenges the popular belief that higher interest rates necessarily drive gold prices lower, presenting historical evidence that no consistent inverse relationship exists.

Key historical data points: During the 1970s, gold prices rose sharply alongside rising interest rates—one-year Treasury bill rates climbed from 3.5% in 1971 to approximately 14.7% in 1981, while gold prices rose from under $200/ounce to a nominal peak of $850/ounce in January 1980, showing a strong positive correlation with T-bill rates. In contrast, the 1980s saw declining rates paired with a gold bear market. The Fed's rate-hiking cycle beginning March 2022 (following Russia's invasion of Ukraine) did coincide with gold tumbling from near $2,000/ounce to a triple bottom around $1,630 by fall 2022, and gold recovered to $1,900 by mid-January 2023 amid expectations of slower rate hikes.

The article identifies several key factors influencing gold prices beyond interest rates: supply and demand dynamics (gold mine supply changes slowly—10+ years from discovery to production—but recycled gold can adjust faster), stock market performance (rising rates typically hurt stocks, potentially pushing investors to gold as a safe haven—gold rose over 60% in 1973-74 while the S&P 500 dropped over 20%), the U.S. dollar's strength (gold is dollar-denominated, so a weaker dollar makes gold more affordable for foreign buyers), central bank purchases, jewelry demand, and inflation concerns.

The article concludes that while it seems logical that Fed funds rate hikes would attract money away from gold into higher-yielding investments, historical data shows no consistent relationship. Supply-and-demand shifts, equity-price moves, and volatility can outweigh the effects of rate changes depending on market conditions. Research has found a significant inverse relationship specifically between real interest rates (not nominal rates) and gold prices in some analyses, with results varying by methodology and period examined.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Some market watchers and investors believe that higher interest rates can send the price of gold lower by increasing the appeal of higher-yielding investments, such as bonds and other fixed-income investments. However, there's not a lot of support for this belief."
</key_excerpts>

## 27 February

* United States ambassador to Israel [Mike Huckabee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Huckabee "Mike Huckabee") emails embassy staff that if they want to leave, they should "do so TODAY"[[1]](#cite_note-1)
* 20:38 [UTC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTC "UTC") – US president [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") gives the order to proceed with Operation Epic Fury.[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4)

## 28 February

### Israeli–US strikes

At 06:35 UTC, [CENTCOM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CENTCOM "CENTCOM") announced that it "and partner forces" had begun airstrikes against Iran.[[5]](#cite_note-Fishbach-5) According to Business Insider, citing a US official, US warships launched [Tomahawk missiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomahawk_missiles "Tomahawk missiles"), the [US Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army "United States Army") used [HIMARS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HIMARS "HIMARS") launchers, and other undisclosed long-range standoff weapons were also used.[[6]](#cite_note-Epstein-6) The US military stated that it used [B-2 stealth bombers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B-2_stealth_bomber "B-2 stealth bomber"), as well as [B-1 Lancers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B-1_Lancers "B-1 Lancers") and [B-52 Stratofortresses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_B-52_Stratofortress "Boeing B-52 Stratofortress"), to strike fortified ballistic missile facilities inside Iran.[[7]](#cite_note-7) At 06:45 UTC,[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] the Israeli Air Force conducted airstrikes that targeted senior Iranian officials. Analysts and news agencies, including Reuters and CNN, described the operation as a 'decapitation strike' or 'leadership-decapitation operation' aimed at the country's top leadership.[[8]](#cite_note-8)[[9]](#cite_note-9) Supreme Leader [Ali Khamenei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ali_Khamenei "Ali Khamenei") and several high officials (attending three meetings at his residential compound) were killed, as were members of his family. According to a statement issued by U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM), the targets of the strikes included Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps [command-and-control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Command_and_control "Command and control") facilities, Iranian air defense systems, missile and drone launch sites, and military airfields.[[10]](#cite_note-10)[[11]](#cite_note-usni-11)

The [Fars News Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fars_News_Agency "Fars News Agency") and [CNN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNN "CNN") reported more explosions across other cities in Iran, including [Qom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qom "Qom"), [Kermanshah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kermanshah "Kermanshah"), [Isfahan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isfahan "Isfahan"), and [Karaj](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karaj "Karaj").[[12]](#cite_note-12)[[13]](#cite_note-13) In Tehran, missile strikes were reported to have occurred on University Street, in the [Jomhouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jomhuri_Eslami_Street "Jomhuri Eslami Street") area, and in the northern [Seyed Khandan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seyed_Khandan "Seyed Khandan") area.[[14]](#cite_note-14) At 07:15 UTC,[[15]](#cite_note-15) The [Shajareh Tayyebeh girls' elementary school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Minab_school_airstrike "2026 Minab school airstrike") in [Minab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minab "Minab"), Iran, was struck by a missile. Iranian media reported 180 killed.[[16]](#cite_note-16)[[17]](#cite_note-17)[[18]](#cite_note-18) A sports hall in [Lamerd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lamerd "Lamerd") was bombed during a girls' practice, killing at least 18 civilians, according to witnesses and Iranian state media.[[19]](#cite_note-19) The IRGC reported that the port city of [Bushehr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bushehr "Bushehr") had also been struck; however, it was unclear whether the [nuclear reactor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bushehr_Nuclear_Power_Plant "Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant") had sustained any damage.[[20]](#cite_note-Iran_International-2026a-20) Rafael Mariano Grossi, the UN nuclear watchdog chief stated that no evidence has been found that nuclear facilities[[21]](#cite_note-21) have been hit from these attacks.[[22]](#cite_note-22)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/10/Attack_on_Lamerd_1_Tasnim_28Feb2026.jpg/250px-Attack_on_Lamerd_1_Tasnim_28Feb2026.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Attack_on_Lamerd_1_Tasnim_28Feb2026.jpg)

Damaged residential area in [Lamerd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lamerd "Lamerd"), southwest Iran, after a reported missile attack targeting local infrastructure

Israel warned Iranian civilians residing near military industries and infrastructure to evacuate immediately, stating "Your presence in these areas puts your life at risk."[[20]](#cite_note-Iran_International-2026a-20) According to [U.S. Central Command](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Central_Command "United States Central Command"), the operation marked the first combat use of [low-cost one-way attack drones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low-cost_Uncrewed_Combat_Attack_System "Low-cost Uncrewed Combat Attack System") based on the Iranian [Shahed 136](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HESA_Shahed_136 "HESA Shahed 136") design.[[11]](#cite_note-usni-11)[[23]](#cite_note-23)[[24]](#cite_note-24) The attacks also used about 200 Israeli fighter jets, in the largest combat sortie in Israel's history,[[25]](#cite_note-25) and the newly developed [Black Sparrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sparrow_(target_missile) "Sparrow (target missile)") air-launched ballistic missile, fired from F-15s.[[26]](#cite_note-26)

A spokesperson for the Iraqi [Popular Mobilization Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_Mobilization_Forces "Popular Mobilization Forces") says that two of its fighters had been killed while three more had been injured during strikes in [Jurf al-Sakhar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jurf_al-Sakhar "Jurf al-Sakhar"), south of [Baghdad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baghdad "Baghdad").[[27]](#cite_note-Mohamed-27)

This is the Wikipedia timeline of the 2026 Iran war, covering the conflict that began on 28 February 2026, part of the broader Middle Eastern crisis (2023–present). The page provides a day-by-day chronological account of military events from 27 February through late August 2026.

Key events covered include:

- **27 February 2026:** US ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee emailed embassy staff urging them to leave "TODAY." At 20:38 UTC, President Donald Trump ordered the start of Operation Epic Fury.

- **28 February 2026:** CENTCOM and partner forces launched airstrikes against Iran at 06:35 UTC. US warships fired Tomahawk missiles, the US Army used HIMARS launchers, and B-2 stealth bombers, B-1 Lancers, and B-52 Stratofortresses struck fortified ballistic missile facilities. At 06:45 UTC, the Israeli Air Force conducted a "decapitation strike" targeting senior Iranian officials. Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and several high officials attending three meetings at his residential compound were killed, along with family members. Targets included IRGC command-and-control facilities, air defense systems, missile/drone launch sites, and military airfields. The Minab girls' elementary school was struck (180 killed per Iranian media) and a Lamerd sports hall was bombed during a girls' practice (at least 18 civilians killed). Iran retaliated at 09:05 UTC with ballistic missiles toward Israel and Gulf states. A missile struck the USN Fifth Fleet.

The timeline is structured by daily entries with sub-sections for US–Israeli strikes, Iranian strikes, the Lebanon theater, and other developments. It covers major operations including the Strait of Hormuz crisis, naval blockade of Iran, Iranian strikes on Arab countries (Bahrain, Jordan, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE), the Lebanon war theater, Khamenei's assassination and succession (with a new leader elected on 9 March), and diplomatic efforts including the Islamabad Talks, Islamabad Memorandum, and the 2026 Iran war ceasefire.

The page includes extensive navigation links to related articles covering the broader 2026 Iran war, including its prelude, analysis, casualties, list of Iranian officials killed, order of battle, regional mobilizations, economic impact, cyberwarfare, regime change efforts, and reactions.

### What is the Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) in Iraq?

The Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), also called al-Hashd al-Shaabi, is a broad coalition of [Iraqi](https://www.britannica.com/place/Iraq) militias that came together in 2014 to fight [ISIS](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Islamic-State-in-Iraq-and-Syria) when the Iraqi army alone was unable to prevent ISIS from taking over broad swathes of the country. The PMF took the lead in defeating ISIS along the Iraqi front. As a result of its success, the Iraqi government formally recognized it as an auxiliary to the armed forces, granting legitimacy to the coalition and salaries to its fighters.

The PMF includes militias from several different political orientations, including Iran-backed [Shiʿi](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Shii) militias, Shiʿi militias that oppose [Iranian](https://www.britannica.com/place/Iran) intervention in Iraq, and militias that represent [Sunni](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Sunni), Christian, and [Yazidi](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Yazidi) communities. The predominant militias are Iranian-backed members of the [Axis of Resistance](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Axis-of-Resistance), including Kataeb Hezbollah, the Badr Organization, ʿAṣāʾib Ahl al-Ḥaqq, and oppose U.S. intervention in Iraq.

Despite the PMF’s status as an auxiliary to the armed forces, it was not fully integrated and some of the constituent militias continue to operate independently of the state, including attacking U.S. forces during periods of tension. Under pressure from the [United States](https://www.britannica.com/place/United-States) in 2026, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi ordered the militias to come under direct state authority.

### Why did Donald Trump declare the ceasefire with Iran over in July 2026?

Since the conclusion of a memorandum of understanding in June 2026 that seeks to end the [Iran war](https://www.britannica.com/event/2026-Iran-war), [Iran](https://www.britannica.com/place/Iran) has repeatedly threatened and attacked ships passing through the [Strait of Hormuz](https://www.britannica.com/place/Strait-of-Hormuz). It hopes to coerce commercial vessels and the international community into following routes and protocols set by Iran that would allow it to control the strait and collect fees on ships passing through. Iran’s activity in the strait has provoked strikes by the [United States](https://www.britannica.com/place/United-States), particularly after three ships were attacked on July 6–7. On July 7, as the United States stepped up strikes against Iranian assets, U.S. Pres. [Donald Trump](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Donald-Trump) said that he considered the truce to be over. The following day he said that the exchange of fire would not lead to long-term military action, but the conflict escalated considerably in the days ahead.

### Why is Iran attacking ships after the June 2026 ceasefire?

Despite the memorandum of understanding (MoU) reached in June 2026 that seeks to reopen the [Strait of Hormuz](https://www.britannica.com/place/Strait-of-Hormuz) and end the [Iran war](https://www.britannica.com/event/2026-Iran-war), [Iran](https://www.britannica.com/place/Iran) sought to assert [hegemonic](https://www.britannica.com/topic/hegemony) control over the strait and eventually collect fees on ships passing through. The country repeatedly warned ships to use preapproved routes and follow protocols set by the regime. It followed up on its threats by firing at multiple ships, including three commercial vessels on July 6–7. Iran’s activity in the strait tested the limits of the MoU and prompted attacks by the [United States](https://www.britannica.com/place/United-States) in response.

### What is Operation Epic Fury?

[Operation Epic Fury](https://www.britannica.com/event/2026-Iran-war) was the [U.S.](https://www.britannica.com/place/United-States) code name for its joint military operations with [Israel](https://www.britannica.com/place/Israel) against [Iran](https://www.britannica.com/place/Iran) that began on February 28, 2026, and concluded on May 5. The opening salvo took out the heart of the Iranian regime, Supreme Leader [Ali Khamenei](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Ali-Khamenei), and triggered a torrent of hundreds of retaliatory missiles and thousands of drones from Iran across the [Middle East](https://www.britannica.com/place/Middle-East). The attacks have left enormous damage, thousands of people dead in Iran, [Lebanon](https://www.britannica.com/place/Lebanon), Israel, and the [Gulf Arab states](https://www.britannica.com/place/Gulf-Arab-States), and millions of people displaced in the region.

### What were the main reasons for tensions between the United States and Iran before the 2026 conflict?

Tensions between the [United States](https://www.britannica.com/place/United-States) and [Iran](https://www.britannica.com/place/Iran) stretch back to the [Islamic Revolution](https://www.britannica.com/event/Iranian-Revolution) in 1979 and the subsequent [Iran hostage crisis](https://www.britannica.com/event/Iran-hostage-crisis), which set a tone of mutual hostility and deep distrust. The immediate concerns leading up to the [2026 Iran war](https://www.britannica.com/event/2026-Iran-war) included Iran’s nuclear program, its [ballistic missiles](https://www.britannica.com/technology/ballistic-missile), its military reach in the [Middle East](https://www.britannica.com/place/Middle-East) region, and failed attempts to [renegotiate a nuclear deal](https://www.britannica.com/event/Iran-nuclear-deal-negotiations) after the collapse of the 2015 [Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action](https://www.britannica.com/event/Joint-Comprehensive-Plan-of-Action) (JCPOA) nuclear agreement.

### How did the United States and Israel begin their military operation against Iran?

On February 28, 2026, [U.S.](https://www.britannica.com/place/United-States) and [Israeli](https://www.britannica.com/place/Israel) forces launched nearly 900 strikes in 12 hours targeting Iranian missiles, air defenses, military infrastructure, and leadership. The initial wave of strikes killed Supreme Leader [Ali Khamenei](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Ali-Khamenei) and dozens of other officials, but it also killed about 170 people when a missile struck a girls’ school adjacent to a naval base in Minab, near [Bandar Abbas](https://www.britannica.com/place/Bandar-Abbas).

### What was Iran’s response to the strikes by the United States and Israel in February 2026?

In response to the attacks by the [United States](https://www.britannica.com/place/United-States) and [Israel](https://www.britannica.com/place/Israel) on [Iran](https://www.britannica.com/place/Iran) on February 28, 2026, Iran launched retaliatory [missile](https://www.britannica.com/technology/missile) and [drone](https://www.britannica.com/technology/unmanned-aerial-vehicle) strikes targeting U.S. embassies, military installations, and oil infrastructure (including vessels in the [Strait of Hormuz](https://www.britannica.com/place/Strait-of-Hormuz)) throughout the [Middle East](https://www.britannica.com/place/Middle-East). Iran hoped its broad retaliation would exact costs and pressure its adversaries into mediation.

### What was the global impact of the 2026 Iran war?

The 2026 Iran war disrupted global travel and trade, halted flights in and out of the [Middle East](https://www.britannica.com/place/Middle-East), and led to shipping reroutes to avoid the [Strait of Hormuz](https://www.britannica.com/place/Strait-of-Hormuz) and the [Red Sea](https://www.britannica.com/place/Red-Sea).

**2026 Iran war**, conflict centered on [Iran](https://www.britannica.com/place/Iran) that was initiated by the [United States](https://www.britannica.com/place/United-States) and [Israel](https://www.britannica.com/place/Israel) on February 28, 2026, and has upended the [dynamics](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/dynamics) of the [Middle East](https://www.britannica.com/place/Middle-East). The opening salvo took out the heart of the Iranian regime, Supreme Leader [Ali Khamenei](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Ali-Khamenei), and triggered a torrent of hundreds of retaliatory missiles and thousands of drones from Iran across the region. The conflict left enormous damage, thousands of people dead in Iran and [Lebanon](https://www.britannica.com/place/Lebanon), dozens dead in Israel and the [Gulf Arab states](https://www.britannica.com/place/Gulf-Arab-States), and millions of people displaced in the region, including more than one-sixth of the population in Lebanon after the [war](https://www.britannica.com/topic/war) prompted the resumption of the [Israel-Hezbollah war](https://www.britannica.com/event/Israel-Hezbollah-war). The danger of crossfire and threats from Iran in particular led to severe disruption of traffic through the [Strait of Hormuz](https://www.britannica.com/place/Strait-of-Hormuz), one of the world’s most [volatile oil](https://www.britannica.com/topic/essential-oil) chokepoints, leading to fuel shortages in parts of Asia and rippling effects across the global economy. After more than five weeks of fighting, the United States and Iran agreed on April 7–8 to a ceasefire that included Israel. In the following weeks the conflict shifted to a game of [brinkmanship](https://www.britannica.com/topic/brinkmanship) between the United States and Iran over restricted access to the Strait of Hormuz. On June 14 mediators announced a [memorandum](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/memorandum) of understanding that was intended to bring the conflict to a formal end within 60 days of its signing, but in July the conflict resumed after Iran struck three commercial vessels that bypassed its preapproved route.

The confrontation took place after years of rising tension over Iran’s nuclear program, its [ballistic missiles](https://www.britannica.com/technology/ballistic-missile), and its military reach across the Middle East. Attempts to [renegotiate a nuclear deal](https://www.britannica.com/event/Iran-nuclear-deal-negotiations) (after the collapse of the [Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action](https://www.britannica.com/event/Joint-Comprehensive-Plan-of-Action) [JCPOA]) in 2025 and 2026 were unsuccessful. Meanwhile, Iran’s posture was in a weakened state after years of sanctions, recent [destabilizing protests](https://www.britannica.com/event/2026-Iranian-Protests), damage inflicted during the [12-day War](https://www.britannica.com/event/12-Day-War) with Israel in June 2025, and the diminished position of Iran’s allies during the [Israel-Hamas War](https://www.britannica.com/event/Israel-Hamas-War). Given Iran’s weakened position, the United States and Israel calculated that they had greater opportunity to advance their objectives through military means than by diplomatic means.

## Conflict

[![Image 20: People stand on rooftops watching a large plume of smoke rise over city buildings after a strike in Tehran at sunset.](https://cdn.britannica.com/06/285406-050-CAB963F0/People-watch-as-smoke-billows-from-strike-on-Tehran-Iran-March-2026.jpg?w=300)](https://cdn.britannica.com/06/285406-050-CAB963F0/People-watch-as-smoke-billows-from-strike-on-Tehran-Iran-March-2026.jpg)

[U.S.-Israeli strikes on Tehran](https://cdn.britannica.com/06/285406-050-CAB963F0/People-watch-as-smoke-billows-from-strike-on-Tehran-Iran-March-2026.jpg)Plume of smoke rising from the Iranian capital, Tehran, from U.S.-Israeli strikes on March 3, 2026.(more)

Midmorning on February 28, U.S. and Israeli forces began conducting joint strikes on Iran, numbering nearly 900 in just the first 12 hours of what the United States dubbed Operation Epic Fury. The attacks targeted Iranian missiles and air defenses, other military [infrastructure](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/infrastructure), and Iranian leadership. According to U.S. and Israeli officials, the timing of the initial attack was tied in part to the ability to target [Ali Khamenei](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Ali-Khamenei), Iran’s [supreme leader](https://www.britannica.com/topic/supreme-leader-of-Iran), before he would go into hiding. Khamenei was killed in the first wave of strikes on February 28, as were dozens of other top Iranian officials. The attacks generated immediate controversy when it was reported that a girls’ school in a town east of [Bandar Abbas](https://www.britannica.com/place/Bandar-Abbas) was struck, killing about 170 people. U.S. forces are believed to have conducted the strikes, according to a preliminary investigation by the U.S. military, while targeting [adjacent](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/adjacent) buildings that belonged to an [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Islamic-Revolutionary-Guard-Corps) (IRGC) naval base.

[![Image 21: People gather near the heavily damaged, partially collapsed building of Iran's Assembly of Experts in Qom, with debris and dust in the street after an airstrike.](https://cdn.britannica.com/13/285413-050-56D046D2/Destroyed-Assembly-of-Experts-Tehran-March-2026.jpg?w=300)](https://cdn.britannica.com/13/285413-050-56D046D2/Destroyed-Assembly-of-Experts-Tehran-March-2026.jpg)

[Disrupting the regime](https://cdn.britannica.com/13/285413-050-56D046D2/Destroyed-Assembly-of-Experts-Tehran-March-2026.jpg)Israeli strikes destroyed the building where Iran's Assembly of Experts was expected on March 3, 2026, delaying Iran's ability to select a new supreme leader after Ali Khamenei was killed.(more)

Iran’s government was quick to prevent a vacuum in leadership, and its swift movement to replace leaders killed in the conflict indicated both the stability of the regime and the resolve of Iran’s hard-liners in the face of conflict. [Ali Larijani](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Ali-Larijani), a broadly trusted senior official who had been serving as the secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, was believed to have been the [de facto](https://www.britannica.com/topic/de-facto) leader of Iran in the immediate aftermath of Khamenei’s death and following preparations to that effect before the war began. [Mojtaba Khamenei](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Mojtaba-Khamenei), who was considered more hawkish and repressive than his father, was appointed supreme leader in early March despite protests from U.S. Pres. [Donald Trump](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Donald-Trump) that he would consider that appointment “unacceptable.” When Larijani was killed on March 17, he was replaced by Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, an appointment that reflected the paramountcy of the IRGC over the political or clerical establishments in Iran’s wartime decision-making.

Meanwhile, retaliatory missile and [drone](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/drone) strikes by Iran embroiled the region. They followed a familiar pattern of horizontal escalation, [according to the international security scholar Robert A. Pape](https://www.foreignaffairs.com/iran/why-escalation-favors-iran) writing in [_Foreign Affairs_](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Foreign-Affairs-journal). Iran’s war strategy widened the arena of conflict, thereby extending the conflict beyond mere military might and into the political and economic realms, with the aim of withstanding bombardment until the conflict would become too costly for the United States and Israel to be willing to sustain. Iranian strikes targeted U.S. embassies and military installations in the [United Arab Emirates](https://www.britannica.com/place/United-Arab-Emirates), [Saudi Arabia](https://www.britannica.com/place/Saudi-Arabia), [Qatar](https://www.britannica.com/place/Qatar), [Kuwait](https://www.britannica.com/place/Kuwait), [Bahrain](https://www.britannica.com/place/Bahrain), [Iraq](https://www.britannica.com/place/Iraq), [Oman](https://www.britannica.com/place/Oman), and [Jordan](https://www.britannica.com/place/Jordan). [NATO](https://www.britannica.com/topic/North-Atlantic-Treaty-Organization) forces struck down Iranian drones and missiles near the Incirlik Air Base in [Turkey](https://www.britannica.com/place/Turkey) (Türkiye).

Iranian attacks also targeted oil infrastructure in the region—including vessels in the [Strait of Hormuz](https://www.britannica.com/place/Strait-of-Hormuz), through which 20 percent of the world’s oil passes—as well as commercial [hubs](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/hubs) in neighboring countries that aid the U.S. military. By late March officials in the IRGC suggested Iran may push its [Houthi](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Houthi-movement) allies in [Yemen](https://www.britannica.com/place/Yemen) to block [Bab el-Mandeb Strait](https://www.britannica.com/place/Bab-El-Mandeb-Strait) to disrupt shipping in the [Red Sea](https://www.britannica.com/place/Red-Sea) and further strain global markets. It remained unclear whether the Houthi movement, which in 2025 had reached a ceasefire with the United States in relation to its attacks on Red Sea shipping, was willing to confront U.S. pressure directly, but on March 28 it launched missiles and drones toward Israel and opened a new front in the expanding regional conflict.

The Strait of Hormuz increasingly became a focal point of the war in March, particularly as other countries hesitated to enter the conflict in order to enforce safe passage. On March 21 Trump threatened to target Iran’s civilian energy infrastructure if Iran did not agree to allow ships to pass through the Strait of Hormuz without interference. He then extended the threat to [Kharg Island](https://www.britannica.com/place/Kharg-Island), the terminal for nearly all of Iran’s oil exports, and to [desalination](https://www.britannica.com/technology/desalination) plants on March 30. Days later he set a deadline for Iran of April 7 and took to [social media](https://www.britannica.com/topic/social-media) with a series of increasingly [vehement](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/vehement) posts. On the morning of April 7 he wrote in one such post that “a whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again.”

## Ceasefire

On April 7–8 Trump announced on social media that he had agreed to a two-week ceasefire brokered by [Pakistan](https://www.britannica.com/place/Pakistan). Moments later, Iranian officials confirmed that Khamenei had approved the ceasefire after a last-minute nudge by [China](https://www.britannica.com/place/China). Transportation through the Strait of Hormuz continued to move at a trickle and remained a major point of [contention](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/contention) in efforts to forge a more lasting ceasefire. Direct negotiations took place in [Islamabad](https://www.britannica.com/place/Islamabad), Pakistan, on April 11–12 between U.S. Vice Pres. [JD Vance](https://www.britannica.com/biography/JD-Vance) and Iranian parliament speaker [Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Mohammad-Bagher-Ghalibaf)—the highest-level direct engagement between the United States and Iran since the [1979 Iranian Revolution](https://www.britannica.com/event/Iranian-Revolution). But when those talks failed to produce an agreement, Trump ordered the [U.S. Navy](https://www.britannica.com/topic/United-States-Navy) to begin a blockade of the strait to prevent the passage of any ships transiting through Iranian ports. As the ceasefire’s two-week deadline came to a close, Trump announced that the United States would continue to [cease](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/cease) fire until the Iranian delegation could present the U.S. delegation with a proposal to end the war that was backed by all factions of the Iranian government. No deadline was set for the extension of the U.S. ceasefire, and proposals put forward by either side to end the war were met with rejection in the weeks ahead.

## Conflict in Lebanon

The conflict also saw the resumption of hostilities between Israel and Iran’s close ally [Hezbollah](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Hezbollah) in [Lebanon](https://www.britannica.com/place/Lebanon), which had been observing a fragile ceasefire since 2024 (_see_[Israel-Hezbollah war](https://www.britannica.com/event/Israel-Hezbollah-war)). Despite the ceasefire, which required the disarmament of Hezbollah and the withdrawal of the [Israel Defense Forces](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Israel-Defense-Forces) (IDF) from southern Lebanon, Hezbollah had been seeking to restore its military [capabilities](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/capabilities) and the IDF had continued to strike targets in southern Lebanon almost daily. After the opening wave of attacks on Iran on February 28, the IDF conducted air strikes on Hezbollah’s infrastructure and warned the militant group against getting involved in the conflict with Iran. On March 2, Hezbollah launched missiles and drones into Israel, prompting an escalation in Israeli air strikes that reached north to southern [Beirut](https://www.britannica.com/place/Beirut). A drone believed to have been launched by Hezbollah also struck a base in [Cyprus](https://www.britannica.com/place/Cyprus) used by the British [Royal Air Force](https://www.britannica.com/topic/The-Royal-Air-Force). In the following days Israel issued sweeping evacuation orders across southern Lebanon, displacing more than 1,100,000 people by late March.

A limited invasion began on March 17 amid reports that a broader ground offensive was likely. On March 24 Israeli minister of defense Israel Katz announced plans for the IDF to occupy southern Lebanon up to the [Litani River](https://www.britannica.com/place/Litani-River-Lebanon), a [swath](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/swath) of territory that the IDF had previously occupied in 1982 during the [Lebanese Civil War](https://www.britannica.com/event/Lebanese-Civil-War) (1975–90) until Israeli forces withdrew in 2000.
